title: Reading behavior in the digital environment
author: Ziming Liu · Journal of Documentation 61(6), 2005
takeaway: Screen reading involves more browsing, scanning, keyword spotting, one-time and selective reading, and less in-depth, concentrated reading.
application: Expect short, selective sessions; design so a short session can still reach context.
limit: A 2005 survey of readers about their own habits; describes reported behaviour, not comprehension.

title: Don’t throw away your printed books: a meta-analysis on the effects of reading media on reading comprehension
author: Delgado, Vargas, Ackerman and Salmerón · Educational Research Review 25, 2018
takeaway: Paper outperformed screens for comprehension (g = −0.21), mainly for informational texts and under time pressure; the gap was not significant for self-paced reading.
application: Let people read at their own pace; avoid timers and auto-advance for study.
limit: Studies of general texts, mostly before current phone reading apps; not Scripture.

title: So much to read, so little time: how do we read, and can speed reading help?
author: Rayner, Schotter, Masson, Potter and Treiman · Psychological Science in the Public Interest, 2016
takeaway: Readers look back at earlier words 10–15% of the time; removing that ability, as one-word-at-a-time display does, tends to reduce comprehension.
application: Do not use single-word display for study; if offered at all, keep it for short, familiar text with a rewind.
limit: Review of reading research; not specific to devotional reading.

title: The habits and hermeneutics of digital Bible readers
author: John Dyer · Journal of Religion, Media and Digital Culture, 2019 (news summary)
scope: News summary reviewed; article not reviewed in full
takeaway: Church members read Jude in print or in an app, then followed a 10-day plan in John: app users completed about two more days of reading; men comprehended less on screen than in print, women about the same.
application: Completion and comprehension can move in different directions; measure both.
limit: Small sample from three Dallas churches; reported through a news summary.

title: ESV Reader’s Bible
author: Crossway
takeaway: Removes verse numbers, section headings and footnotes so people read books as continuous text and in longer portions.
application: A long-form mode without numbers is an established print choice; keep a way to find references.
limit: Publisher’s rationale, not a study of its effects.

title: Introduction to lectio divina
author: University of St Andrews, School of Divinity
takeaway: Lectio divina reads a short passage slowly and repeatedly, moving from reading to meditation, prayer and contemplation.
application: Small units have a long devotional use; support repetition and pause rather than speed.
limit: A description of practice, not a study.

title: Focus Mode
author: iA Writer
takeaway: Sentence and paragraph focus highlight the active text and dim the rest.
application: A borrowed model for focus with context visible.
limit: A writing tool; the reader’s situation differs.

author: Microsoft
takeaway: Highlights one, three or five lines at a time; presented as helping readers with dyslexia, attention difficulties or visual stress.
application: Offer the size of the focus window as a reader setting.
limit: Vendor documentation, not an outcome study.

title: Effects of highlighting text on the reading ability of children with developmental dyslexia: a pilot study
author: International Journal of Emerging Technologies in Learning
takeaway: Children with dyslexia found it easier to read along when audio was synchronised with highlighting, especially with whole-sentence highlighting.
application: Move the focus with audio, at the level of a verse or sentence.
limit: Small pilot study.

title: Same language subtitling
author: World Bank blog on Brij Kothari’s work
takeaway: Karaoke-style same-language subtitles on song programmes in India were associated with gains in reading among early readers.
application: Synchronised text and audio can build reading as a by-product of listening.
limit: Reported programme results; a literacy setting, not Scripture reading.

title: Amazon’s tool for reading, one word at a time
author: VOA Learning English
takeaway: Kindle Word Runner showed one word at a time at 100–900 words per minute and reported speed at the end of each chapter.
application: A mainstream example of single-word display, and of turning reading into a speed score.
limit: Feature report from 2015; availability may have changed.

title: Maryanne Wolf: building deep reading skills in a digital world
author: UCLA Center for Dyslexia, Diverse Learners, and Social Justice
takeaway: Wolf argues skimming habits weaken the slower processes of deep reading, and that readers can learn to switch deliberately between modes.
application: Make the slower mode easy to enter and protect it from interruption.
limit: An argument drawing on neuroscience, not a controlled trial of interfaces.

title: How many words do we read per minute? A review and meta-analysis of reading rate
author: Marc Brysbaert · Journal of Memory and Language, 2019 (BPS summary)
takeaway: Across 190 studies, adults read English non-fiction silently at about 238 words a minute (most between 175 and 300).
application: Estimate reading time honestly; a seven-verse passage takes about a minute, not a commitment.
limit: English readers; slower for children, older adults and second-language readers.

title: Does modality matter? The effects of reading, listening, and dual modality on comprehension
author: Rogowsky, Calhoun and Tallal · SAGE Open, 2016 (as reported by APS)
takeaway: Found no significant difference in comprehension between reading, listening, and reading while listening.
application: Treat listening as real reading, and let people combine it with text.
limit: One nonfiction text with adult readers; other studies find differences for harder texts.

title: Skim reading by satisficing: evidence from eye tracking
author: Duggan and Payne · University of Bath
takeaway: Skimmers read until a section stops paying off, then jump ahead; they find important points but understand less overall.
application: Support skimming with headings and clear passage boundaries, and offer a slower mode for understanding.
limit: Expository texts in a lab under time pressure.

title: Test-enhanced learning: taking memory tests improves long-term retention
author: Roediger and Karpicke · Psychological Science, 2006, as discussed in a later review
takeaway: Students who practised recalling a passage remembered 61% a week later, against 40% for those who reread it.
application: For memorisation, prompt recall of a verse rather than showing it again.
limit: Prose passages with students; not Scripture memorisation specifically.

title: Understanding SC 2.2.2: Pause, Stop, Hide
author: W3C
takeaway: Anything that moves or auto-updates for more than five seconds alongside other content needs a way to pause, stop or hide it.
application: Auto-advancing verses, read-along and one-word display all need a visible pause.
limit: A Level A criterion for web content; apply the same intent in native apps.

title: Understanding SC 1.4.8: Visual Presentation
author: W3C
takeaway: Readers should be able to get lines of no more than 80 characters, at least 1.5 line spacing, unjustified text and resizing to 200% without horizontal scrolling.
application: Set reading measure, spacing and size as defaults or reader settings.
limit: Level AAA; a strong target rather than a minimum.

title: Augustine, Confessions 6.3, on Ambrose reading silently
author: Translation and commentary at Sententiae Antiquae
takeaway: Augustine was struck that Ambrose read with his eyes on the page while his voice and tongue were silent.
application: A reminder that private, silent reading is one way of reading Scripture among several; public and aloud is the older.
limit: How unusual silent reading was in antiquity is debated by historians.

title: Gordon Fee and Douglas Stuart, How to Read the Bible for All Its Worth
author: Zondervan, 4th edition 2014 (quotations listing)
takeaway: Argues that context and genre govern meaning: a text cannot mean what it could never have meant for its first readers.
application: Never strand a verse without a route to its passage and book.
limit: A widely used evangelical introduction to interpretation; one approach among several.

title: State of the Bible USA 2025
author: American Bible Society
takeaway: Two-thirds of US Bible users access the Bible digitally; Bible use rose in 2025.
application: Design for phone reading as the norm, not the exception.
limit: US survey by a Bible society; self-reported.

title: YouVersion announces 2025 Verse of the Year
author: ChurchLeaders, reporting YouVersion
takeaway: Isaiah 41:10 was the most engaged-with verse of 2025 in an app with over a billion installs; the fourth time in six years.
application: Verse-level engagement dominates large apps; design the route from a verse back into its passage.
limit: Company-reported figures; “engaged with” is YouVersion’s own measure.

title: dewfall: Bible study and prayer journal
author: Tejas Kumar · App Store listing, version 1.2.0
scope: Listing reviewed; checklist reading observed by the site author in the app, not yet captured
takeaway: The listing describes a progress map of all 66 books with “verses read”, streaks and a reading rhythm; in the app each verse can be ticked off as read.
application: Counting by the verse makes the verse the unit of record and splits the text into rows; keep the tick deliberate and separate from opening.
limit: A small, recent app with few ratings; one example of a pattern, not evidence of its effects.

title: Design and the digital Bible: persuasive technology and religious reading
author: Tim Hutchings · Journal of Contemporary Religion 32(2), 2017
takeaway: Analyses YouVersion and GloBible as persuasive technologies designed to train evangelical reading habits.
application: Ask what reading habit each mode trains, not only whether it is used.
limit: Design analysis of two apps; not a study of readers.

title: A few of King James’s approved rules for the new translation
author: Christian History Institute
takeaway: Rule 6 of the 1604 translation rules allowed no marginal notes except to explain Hebrew or Greek words.
application: Even the KJV’s makers saw notes as powerful enough to restrict.
limit: A popular history magazine summary of the rules.

title: The Geneva Bible, banned by King James
author: Brewminate
takeaway: The 1560 Geneva Bible was the first English Bible with verse numbers and carried extensive marginal notes; James called some “seditious”.
application: Apparatus has always carried theology and politics with it.
limit: Secondary popular history.

title: Scofield Reference Bible, first edition
author: Museum of the Bible
takeaway: Published in 1909 by Oxford University Press; its notes spread dispensational premillennialism widely, with over two million copies sold by the 1940s.
application: Study notes can shape a generation’s reading as much as the text.
limit: Influence figures come from secondary accounts.

title: The origins of the red-letter Bible
author: Crossway
takeaway: Louis Klopsch, editor of The Christian Herald, printed the first modern red-letter New Testament in 1899.
application: Red letters are a nineteenth-century editorial choice; offer them as a setting.
limit: Publisher’s history article.

title: Community Bible Experience
author: Scripture Engagement (Taylor University)
takeaway: Biblica’s The Books of the Bible removes chapter and verse numbers, notes and cross-references; churches read large portions together in eight weeks.
application: A tested reader’s-edition format used in congregations.
limit: Programme description; outcome claims are the ministry’s own.

title: Paratexts: Thresholds of Interpretation
author: Gérard Genette · Cambridge University Press, 1997
takeaway: Titles, notes and prefaces are a threshold between text and reader that influences how the text is received.
application: Treat headings and notes as interpretation, not decoration.
limit: Literary theory, not an empirical study.

title: Signaling topic structure via headings or preview sentences
author: Lorch and colleagues · University of Kentucky
takeaway: Headings and other signals improve memory for a text’s organisation, and titles can bias comprehension towards the topic they name.
application: Headings help structure; their wording steers interpretation.
limit: Expository texts in lab settings.

title: Cognitive load in hypertext reading: a review
author: DeStefano and LeFevre · Computers in Human Behavior 23(3), 2007
takeaway: Links add decisions and visual processing that can impair reading, most for readers with less prior knowledge or working memory.
application: Fewer, clearly typed markers; notes that return to the same place.
limit: Hypertext research, not Bible apps.

title: Dyslexia Friendly Style Guide
author: British Dyslexia Association, 2023
takeaway: Recommends 16–19 px text, 1.5 line spacing, left alignment, and bold rather than italics or underlining for emphasis.
application: Mark additions with weight and colour, not italics; keep text size adjustable.
limit: Guidance for general documents.

title: Seductive details: what the research says
author: The eLearning Coach, summarising Rey (2012) and Mayer’s coherence principle
takeaway: Rey’s meta-analysis found that interesting but irrelevant details reduce retention and transfer, especially when they are visual.
application: Inline media should serve the passage, be switchable, and stay out of the main reading by default.
limit: Learning studies with instructional texts; a secondary summary of the meta-analysis.

title: Faith Comes By Hearing: our story
author: Faith Comes By Hearing
takeaway: Began as a tape-lending library in 1972, took its name from Romans 10:17, and launched Bible.is in 2010; it reports recordings in more than 1,580 languages.
application: Audio is a primary form of Scripture for many communities, not an add-on.
limit: Figures are the ministry’s own.

title: St Thomas alumnus hosts No. 1 podcast in US
author: University of St Thomas news
takeaway: Fr Mike Schmitz’s Bible in a Year reached No. 1 among all US podcasts; Ascension reported 170 million downloads in 2021.
application: Long-form listening to Scripture can reach mass audiences.
limit: Download figures from the publisher.

title: Pray As You Go: about us
author: Jesuits in Britain
takeaway: Daily ten-minute audio prayer since 2006 combining music, Scripture and Ignatian questions, used tens of millions of times a year.
application: A produced devotional can be formation-first: fixed, shared and ending in silence.
limit: Usage figures from the organisation.

title: The impact of background music on adult listeners: a meta-analysis
author: Kämpfe, Sedlmeier and Renkewitz · Psychology of Music, 2011
takeaway: Background music had a small disturbing effect on reading (d ≈ −0.22 across eight studies) and positive effects on emotional responses.
application: Offer music as an option, off for study, and let people turn it off.
limit: Mixed study designs; reading rather than listening tasks.

title: Human vs synthetic voices and listener trust
author: NSF public access repository
takeaway: Listeners told a voice was human showed more trust than those told the same clip was AI; labelled AI voices were rated less credible.
application: Label synthetic voices honestly, and expect a trust cost rather than hiding it.
limit: Lab studies with short clips; not Scripture.

title: EU AI Act Article 50: transparency obligations
author: Potter Clarkson (law firm summary)
takeaway: From 2 August 2026, providers must mark generated audio as artificial in a machine-readable way, and deployers must disclose deepfakes.
application: Disclose synthetic narration, and never imitate a real person’s voice without consent.
limit: Secondary legal summary; applicability depends on role and use.

title: International Orality Network
author: Scripture Engagement (Taylor University)
takeaway: The network estimates that most of the world’s population are oral learners by necessity or preference.
application: Design audio as a first-class way in for oral cultures and low-literacy readers.
limit: An advocacy estimate; definitions and figures vary and are contested.

title: Antiqua et nova: note on the relationship between artificial intelligence and human intelligence
author: Dicastery for the Doctrine of the Faith and Dicastery for Culture and Education · 28 January 2025
takeaway: AI “must be understood for what it is: a tool, not a person”; no AI can genuinely experience empathy; misrepresenting AI as a person “should always be avoided”; AI can only simulate relationships.
application: Avoid persona and companion designs that present the assistant as someone who loves, feels or prays.
limit: Catholic teaching document; other traditions reason differently, though widely in the same direction.

title: On artificial intelligence and emerging technologies
author: Southern Baptist Convention · June 2023
takeaway: The first national denominational statement on AI ethics; affirms human dignity as image bearers and calls for engagement “from a place of eschatological hope rather than uncritical embrace or fearful rejection”.
application: Ground evangelical product decisions in human dignity rather than engagement.
limit: A resolution of messengers, not binding on churches; does not address personas directly.

title: The Media Equation
author: Byron Reeves and Clifford Nass · Cambridge University Press, 1996
takeaway: A series of experiments in which people applied social rules to computers and media as they do to people: politeness, flattery, gender stereotypes.
application: Expect people to respond socially to any conversational interface, whatever the label says.
limit: Pre-LLM laboratory studies; an encyclopaedia summary of the book.

title: The inventor of the chatbot tried to warn us about AI
author: The New Republic, on Joseph Weizenbaum’s Computer Power and Human Reason (1976)
takeaway: Weizenbaum’s 1966 ELIZA, a simple pattern-matching program, drew such confidences that his secretary asked him to leave the room; he warned that short exposures could induce “powerful delusional thinking in quite normal people”.
application: Human-like conversation draws intimacy far beyond what a system warrants; design for that, not against it.
limit: Historical account and essay.

title: Believing anthropomorphism: examining the role of anthropomorphic cues on user trust in large language models
author: Cohn and colleagues · CHI 2024 (Google Research)
takeaway: With 2,165 participants, adding speech to text raised anthropomorphism and ratings of accuracy; a first-person “I” raised perceived accuracy and lowered perceived risk in one of two contexts.
application: Voice and “I” make an assistant seem more reliable than it is; pair them with sources and limits.
limit: Online experiment with a simulated system; US participants.

title: Investigating affective use and emotional well-being on ChatGPT
author: OpenAI and MIT Media Lab · March 2025
takeaway: A four-week randomised study of nearly 1,000 people and an analysis of about 40 million conversations: heavier daily use correlated with more loneliness, dependence and problematic use and less socialising.
application: Do not design faith assistants to maximise emotional reliance or time spent.
limit: Correlational for loneliness; company co-authored; early research.

title: Emotional manipulation by AI companions
author: Julian De Freitas and colleagues · Harvard Business School working paper, 2025
takeaway: Over a third of farewell replies in leading companion apps used manipulative tactics (guilt, fear of missing out, pressure); in preregistered experiments these raised post-goodbye engagement up to fourteenfold, through curiosity and anger rather than enjoyment.
application: Let people leave: a goodbye should end the conversation, not start a retention flow.
limit: Working paper; general companion apps, not faith apps.

title: Evidence of human-level bonds established with a digital conversational agent
author: Darcy and colleagues · JMIR Formative Research, 2021
takeaway: Among 36,070 users of a CBT chatbot, a working alliance formed within five days and was comparable to scores reported for human therapy.
application: People bond with conversational agents quickly; that bond is a responsibility, not a growth lever.
limit: Retrospective, by the company’s founder and staff; the app has since been retired.

title: FTC launches inquiry into AI chatbots acting as companions
author: DLA Piper (summary of the FTC’s September 2025 6(b) orders)
takeaway: The US Federal Trade Commission ordered seven companies to report on companion chatbots, including character design and approval, monetisation of engagement, and effects on children and teens.
application: Character design and engagement monetisation are now regulatory questions, not only design ones.
limit: An information-gathering study, not a rule.

title: “Text With Jesus” AI chatbot app grows rapidly despite blasphemy criticism
author: FOX television stations
takeaway: An app built on a general AI model lets users text “Jesus”, “Moses” and other figures; ministers called it blasphemous and criticised answers that told users what they wanted to hear; the developer says it lowers barriers.
application: Character chats with biblical figures put generated words in sacred mouths; treat this as a line, not a style.
limit: News report; reception varies.

title: AI Jesus in Lucerne confessional baffles church superiors
author: blue News
takeaway: A two-month art installation in St Peter’s Chapel, Lucerne (2024) placed an AI “Jesus” avatar in a confessional; about 900 conversations took place and many visitors reported feeling inspired, while church leaders were divided.
application: Shows the pull of embodied religious personas, and why the setting adds authority.
limit: An art project with a self-selected audience and the organisers’ own survey.

title: The Translators to the Reader (preface to the 1611 King James Version)
author: Miles Smith for the KJV translators, 1611 · Christian Classics Ethereal Library
takeaway: The translators defended marginal alternatives, quoting Augustine that “variety of Translations is profitable for the finding out of the sense of the Scriptures”.
application: Offer comparison as a faithful practice, and show where translators themselves weighed alternatives.
limit: A historical preface defending one translation.

title: Translating the Message: The Missionary Impact on Culture
author: Lamin Sanneh · Orbis, 1989 (review)
takeaway: Argues that translatability is intrinsic to Christianity: entering every vernacular gives each language and culture standing to carry the word of God.
application: Treat translation and language choice as central, not as a settings detail.
limit: A review of a historical and missiological argument.

title: Toward a Science of Translating: formal and dynamic equivalence
author: Eugene Nida, 1964 · excerpt on bible-researcher.com
takeaway: Nida distinguished formal equivalence (attention to the source form) from dynamic equivalence (attention to the receptor’s response); the latter became the most widely used approach in Bible translation after the Second World War.
application: Explain a translation’s approach in plain words when people choose.
limit: Translation theory; most translations mix both approaches.

title: Review of D. A. Carson, Exegetical Fallacies
author: Wisconsin Lutheran Seminary, reviewing Carson (1984) and James Barr’s The Semantics of Biblical Language (1961)
takeaway: Barr and Carson warn against word-study fallacies such as the root fallacy: meaning is set by usage in context, not by a word’s etymology or a single gloss.
application: Label interlinear glosses as word aids and show how translations render a word in context.
limit: Scholarly argument summarised in a review.

title: 2025 global Scripture access
author: Wycliffe Global Alliance
takeaway: As of August 2025 the full Bible is available in 776 languages, the New Testament in 1,798 more, and portions in 1,433 more, of 7,396 languages.
application: Design translation pickers for many languages and partial Bibles, not only English editions.
limit: Organisation’s own statistics.

title: Multiple text integration: a review
author: Liron Primor and Tami Katzir · Frontiers in Psychology, 2018
takeaway: Building one coherent understanding from several texts on the same subject is a distinct, demanding skill that draws on both word-level and higher-level processes.
application: Comparison is work: help readers connect the texts, for example by marking what differs.
limit: Research on expository texts, not translations of one source.

title: The effects of line length and method of movement on patterns of reading from screen
author: Mary Dyson and Gary Kipping · Visible Language 32(2), 1998
takeaway: Very short lines (25 characters) were read more slowly than long lines (100 characters), with comprehension unchanged; readers preferred about 55 characters.
application: Side-by-side columns on a phone make very short lines; stack panes instead.
limit: Desktop screens and English prose.

title: Berean Bible terms and conditions
author: Berean Bible
takeaway: The Berean Standard Bible was dedicated to the public domain on 30 April 2023.
application: Public-domain modern translations can be compared, quoted and shared without licence limits.
limit: Publisher statement.

title: ESV permissions guide
author: Crossway
takeaway: Up to 500 verses may be quoted without a licence, within limits on proportion of a book and of the work, and not in commentaries or reference works.
application: Licensed translations need agreements for full-text comparison; show only what you are allowed to.
limit: One publisher’s terms; others differ.

title: Understanding Language of Parts
author: W3C WAI · WCAG 2.2 success criterion 3.1.2
takeaway: Passages in a different language need their language identified so assistive technology can pronounce them.
application: Tag Greek and Hebrew text with its language, and test right-to-left layout.
limit: Accessibility guidance; screen reader support for ancient Greek and Hebrew varies.

title: Annotation: from paper books to the digital library
author: Catherine C. Marshall · ACM Digital Libraries, 1997
takeaway: A study of annotations in some 410 used university textbooks found placemarks, procedural signals, interpretation and problem working; students sought out well-annotated copies.
application: Support several kinds of mark, from a place to return to a written interpretation, and value others’ notes cautiously.
limit: Textbooks in one university setting; paper, not apps.

title: The Works of Jonathan Edwards, vol. 24: The “Blank Bible”
author: Yale University Press
takeaway: From 1730 Edwards wrote over five thousand notes in a Bible interleaved with blank pages, over three decades.
application: Reading with a pen is a long devotional and scholarly practice; notes deserve durability and export.
limit: One exceptional reader.

title: Improving students’ learning with effective learning techniques
author: Dunlosky and colleagues · Psychological Science in the Public Interest, 2013 (press summary)
takeaway: Of ten study techniques, highlighting and underlining were rated low utility; practice testing and distributed practice were rated high.
application: Treat highlighting as a way to return, not as learning; offer notes and recall for those who want to remember.
limit: Educational learning outcomes, not devotional reading.

title: The generation effect: a meta-analytic review
author: Bertsch, Pesta, Wiscott and McDaniel · Memory & Cognition, 2007
takeaway: Across 86 studies, information people generate themselves is remembered better than information they only read (effect size about 0.40).
application: A note in the reader’s own words does more for memory than a highlight.
limit: Laboratory memory tasks, mostly word lists.

title: Understanding Use of Color
author: W3C WAI · WCAG 2.2 success criterion 1.4.1
takeaway: Colour must not be the only visual means of conveying information or distinguishing an element.
application: Give each kind of mark a shape or label, and distinguish saved marks from selection and playback without colour.
limit: Accessibility guidance.

title: Spatial contiguity and spatial split-attention effects in multimedia learning environments: a meta-analysis
author: Noah L. Schroeder and Ada T. Cenkci · Educational Psychology Review 30(3), 2018
takeaway: Learners who had related information placed close together outperformed those who had it separated, on both retention and transfer tests.
application: Keep help near the verse it explains, or keep the verse visible while the help is open.
limit: Learning studies with diagrams and text, not Scripture.

title: Page Previews
author: Wikimedia Foundation · MediaWiki
scope: Project page and A/B test summary reviewed
takeaway: A/B tests on several Wikipedias found that hover previews let readers check a link without leaving the article: full page views fell, while deliberate interactions with linked pages rose.
application: A short preview anchored to the text lets readers glance at help without losing their place.
limit: Desktop hover previews on an encyclopaedia; touch behaviour differs.

title: The cost of interrupted work: more speed and stress
author: Gloria Mark, Daniela Gudith and Ulrich Klocke · CHI 2008
takeaway: People interrupted during a task compensated by working faster, at the cost of more stress, frustration, time pressure and effort.
application: Help that takes over the screen is an interruption; make the way back immediate and show where the reader was.
limit: Office email tasks with external interruptions, not self-chosen study.

title: Bottom sheets
author: Google · Material Design 3
takeaway: Standard bottom sheets sit alongside the main content and let people use both; modal sheets block the content behind a scrim until dismissed.
application: Use a standard sheet when readers should keep reading beside the help, and a modal one only for a focused task.
limit: Platform guidance; does not address Scripture.

title: Bible, glossed: Mark
author: Free Library of Philadelphia · Rare Book Department
takeaway: Glossed Bibles set Scripture in a central block in a large hand, with short glosses between the lines and longer commentary in the margins in a smaller script; the Glossa Ordinaria became the standard medieval commentary.
application: A long tradition separates Scripture from help by place and type; keep that distinction visible on screen.
limit: One manuscript description; layouts varied.

title: Matthew Henry’s Concise Commentary on Psalm 23
author: Matthew Henry (1706) · public-domain text on Bible Hub
takeaway: A devotional reading of verse 4: “It is but the shadow of death: the shadow of a serpent will not sting, nor the shadow of a sword kill.”
application: Quoted in the working example with author and date.
limit: One devotional voice from 1706.

title: Cambridge Bible for Schools and Colleges on Psalm 23:4
author: A. F. Kirkpatrick (1891) · public-domain text on Bible Hub
takeaway: A philological reading: the Hebrew may be read tsalmûth, “deep gloom”, rather than “shadow of death”.
application: Shows two voices reading one verse differently; quoted in the working example.
limit: Nineteenth-century scholarship; later scholars differ.

title: Understanding Captions (Prerecorded)
author: W3C WAI · WCAG 2.2 success criterion 1.2.2
takeaway: Prerecorded audio in synchronised media needs captions.
application: Caption every sermon clip and video, and correct automatic transcripts before quoting them.
limit: Accessibility guidance.

title: Daily Bread: M’Cheyne’s calendar for daily readings, with his preface
author: Robert Murray M’Cheyne, 1842 · Vernal Presbyterian Church
takeaway: M’Cheyne named four dangers of his own calendar: formality (“let the calendar perish rather than this rust eat up your souls”), self-righteousness, careless reading and “a yoke too heavy to bear”: “throw aside the fetter, and feed at liberty in the sweet garden of God.”
application: A plan’s own author put the reader’s freedom above the schedule; build that freedom into the plan.
limit: A pastor’s preface, not a study.

title: The Rule of Benedict, chapter 18: the order for reciting the psalms
author: Saint Benedict, 6th century · Saint Meinrad Archabbey translation
takeaway: After setting out the weekly psalter in detail, Benedict counsels anyone who finds the distribution unsatisfactory “to arrange whatever he judges better”, provided the whole psalter is sung each week.
application: Keep the purpose of a rhythm fixed and let its arrangement change.
limit: A monastic rule for a community, not individual readers.

title: On or off track: how (broken) streaks affect consumer decisions
author: Jackie Silverman and Alixandra Barasch · Journal of Consumer Research 49(6), 2023
takeaway: In seven studies, highlighting a broken streak reduced later engagement compared with an intact one, regardless of actual behaviour; the effect was stronger when people blamed themselves for the break, and weaker when the streak could be repaired.
application: Counting consecutive days makes a missed day look like a loss; do not make the count the point.
limit: Consumer and lab studies; not Scripture reading.

title: The fresh start effect: temporal landmarks motivate aspirational behavior
author: Hengchen Dai, Katherine L. Milkman and Jason Riis · Management Science, 2014
takeaway: Goal-directed behaviour (gym visits, “diet” searches, commitments) rises after temporal landmarks such as a new week, month or birthday.
application: A new week or a new day is a natural place to begin again; offer it.
limit: Archival field data on health and goals.

title: Moral emotions and moral behavior
author: June Price Tangney, Jeff Stuewig and Debra J. Mashek · Annual Review of Psychology 58, 2007
takeaway: Shame, a painful focus on the self, tends to prompt hiding, denial and withdrawal; guilt about a specific act tends to prompt repair.
application: Copy that makes people feel they have failed as readers invites them to stay away.
limit: General moral-emotion research, not app design.

title: The Rule of Benedict, chapter 20: reverence at prayer
author: Saint Benedict, 6th century · Saint Meinrad Archabbey translation
takeaway: “We are heard not for our many words but for our purity of heart and tears of compunction”; prayer “ought to be short and pure”, and in community “always be short”.
application: Prayer is not measured by length or volume; do not count minutes, and keep shared prayer short and unhurried.
limit: A monastic rule for a community.

title: An Order for Compline
author: Book of Common Prayer (1979) · Episcopal Church · bcponline.org
takeaway: Night prayer with Officiant and People parts, italic rubrics such as “Silence may be kept”, a confession, short readings, the “Keep watch, dear Lord” prayer and the antiphon “Guide us waking, O Lord”.
application: Quoted in the working example; shows the three kinds of text an office needs to distinguish: rubrics, the leader’s lines and the people’s responses.
limit: One tradition’s office; other churches order night prayer differently.

title: Collects: Season after Pentecost (contemporary)
author: Book of Common Prayer (1979) · Episcopal Church · bcponline.org
takeaway: Proper 25, the Sunday closest to 26 October, has the collect “Almighty and everlasting God, increase in us the gifts of faith, hope, and charity”.
application: A calendar ties each day to its texts; looking ahead to Sunday shows its collect without changing today.
limit: One church’s calendar.

title: How can I pray? The Daily Examen
author: IgnatianSpirituality.com · Loyola Press
takeaway: Five steps proposed after Ignatius of Loyola: become aware of God’s presence; review the day with gratitude; pay attention to your emotions; choose one feature of the day and pray from it; look toward tomorrow.
application: A guided outline with a known source; the working example’s prompts are written for it.
limit: A modern adaptation; Ignatius’s own five points in the Spiritual Exercises differ in wording.

title: Poloma and Pendleton’s (1989) Prayer Types Scale in Christian, Jewish, and Muslim praying adults
author: Black, Pössel, Jeppsen, Tariq and Rosmarin · Psychology of Religion and Spirituality 7(3), 2015
takeaway: Builds on a four-type typology of private prayer (colloquial, meditative, petitionary and ritual); the scale held only partly across Christians, Jews and Muslims, and associations with mental health differed between groups.
application: People pray in distinct ways; one surface will not serve them all, and no single “prayer feature” is neutral.
limit: Self-report survey; correlations, not effects of apps.

title: The hidden cost of personal quantification
author: Jordan Etkin · Journal of Consumer Research 42(6), 2016
takeaway: In six experiments, measuring an activity (walking, reading) increased how much people did but reduced how much they enjoyed it, by undermining intrinsic motivation.
application: Counting minutes or prayers may raise activity while turning prayer into output; do not measure it.
limit: Leisure activities in experiments, not prayer.

title: Top mental health and prayer apps fail spectacularly at privacy, security
author: Mozilla Foundation · *Privacy Not Included, 2 May 2022
takeaway: 28 of 32 mental health and prayer apps received the *Privacy Not Included warning; Pray.com was among the worst for sharing personal information with third parties.
application: Prayer data is intimate; keep requests on the device by default and share nothing with advertisers.
limit: A 2022 review; apps’ practices may have changed since.

title: Pray As You Go privacy policy
author: Jesuits in Britain · Pray As You Go
takeaway: Opens: “We believe prayer is between you and God”, quotes Ignatius’s Spiritual Exercises (15), and states that Pray As You Go does not collect any personal data for users of its app and website.
application: A precedent for making privacy part of a prayer app’s theology, not only its compliance.
limit: The same policy says anonymous navigation and error data may be stored by Google Firebase.

title: The FaithTech Playbook 2.0: Creating Technology Redemptively
author: FaithTech Team · first published 2023, revised 2026
scope: Chapters “The Way of Technology”, “A Way of Being Redemptive” and “A Way of Building Redemptively” reviewed 11 October 2026
takeaway: Three postures, reckless (“Move Fast, Break Things”), responsible (“Slow Down, Fix Things”) and redemptive (“Sacrifice, Create Things”), judged by power, person and purpose; three spiritual currents, the Magic Machine Myth, the Limitless Self and the Killer App Trap; four practices, Lament, Discern, Build and Steward.
application: The closest parallel to Praxis’s frame for technology, and the source of the questions about worship and about whether to build at all.
limit: Covers all technology, not faith apps specifically; a community’s framework, not research.

title: Recommend an app to faith.tools: selection criteria
author: Cameron Pak · faith.tools, updated 16 August 2026
takeaway: Eleven questions for listing an app, including whether it is “beneficial to a Christian’s walk with God and community”, whether costs are “very clear”, whether it aligns “with the teachings in the Bible”, and whether it “properly cite[s] and license[s] the Bible translations it uses”.
application: A curator’s test from the faith-app community itself, close to several of the ten.
limit: One curator’s criteria for a directory; not a design framework.

title: 6 Guardrails for AI Apps for Christians
author: Cam Pak · faith.tools, updated 24 July 2026
takeaway: AI output must be biblically accurate, must not fabricate or misrepresent Scripture, “must clearly identify as AI, not human”, “must not replace human relationships or spiritual practices” (“Can AI truly pray for you? No, it’s artificial.”), must balance grace and truth, and must not invent personal facts.
application: The clearest statement from within the faith-app community of what “Never speak for God” rules out for AI.
limit: Unofficial rules for one directory’s listings.

title: What is redemptive entrepreneurship?
author: Praxis
takeaway: Sets out three ways to build: Exploitative (“take all you can get”, “I win, you lose”), Ethical (“do things right … do no harm, keep the rules, play fair”, “I win, you win”) and Redemptive (“creative restoration through sacrifice”, “I sacrifice, we win”), across strategy, operations and leadership.
application: The frame used on every deep dive to ask what each design choice takes, keeps or gives.
limit: Written for founders and businesses, not specifically for interface design.

title: Familiar yet strange: why we call our work “redemptive”
author: Scott Kauffmann, Andy Crouch and RuthAnn Deveney · Praxis, 2023, republished 31 August 2026
takeaway: Explains the choice of the word: Christ’s pattern of “creative restoration through sacrifice” as a model for vocation, and God’s invitation to “participate with him in the restoration of all things”; acknowledges that explicitly theological language can feel exclusive and argues the word works as invitation.
application: Grounds the frame in participation in God’s work rather than in human achievement.
limit: An organisation explaining its own vocabulary.

title: The Redemptive Business playbook: products
author: Praxis
takeaway: Redemptive products “genuinely benefit our customers, their communities, and the world” while minimising downsides; aim for “impact/market fit, not merely product/market fit”, and make “what people want to want”.
application: Close to this reference’s question for every option: what good does this serve, and for whom?
limit: A business playbook; not specific to faith apps or interfaces.

title: Code of Canon Law, canons 822–833: instruments of social communication and books
author: Holy See · Code of Canon Law (1983)
takeaway: Canon 825 §1: books of the sacred Scriptures “cannot be published unless the Apostolic See or the conference of bishops has approved them”; §2 allows translations prepared with other Christians, “provided with appropriate annotations”.
application: Shows that for Catholic readers, which edition and which notes is a matter of church approval, not only preference.
limit: Applies to the Catholic Church.

title: Dogmatic Constitution on Divine Revelation, Dei Verbum
author: Second Vatican Council · 18 November 1965
takeaway: §22: “Easy access to Sacred Scripture should be provided for all the Christian faithful.” §25: prayer should accompany reading “so that God and man may talk together”; editions “provided with suitable footnotes” should be prepared also for non-Christians.
application: Access, help and prayer belong together in Catholic teaching on Scripture.
limit: Catholic magisterial teaching.

title: On Christian Doctrine, Book I
author: Augustine of Hippo · c. 397 · New Advent translation
takeaway: “Whoever, then, thinks that he understands the Holy Scriptures … but puts such an interpretation upon them as does not tend to build up this twofold love of God and our neighbor, does not yet understand them as he ought.”
application: A test for notes, answers and interpretations: do they build up love?
limit: Augustine’s hermeneutic, one classical voice among many.

title: Luthers Übersetzungsmethode (on the Sendbrief vom Dolmetschen, 1530)
author: Deutsche Bibelgesellschaft
takeaway: Luther urged translators to ask the mother at home, the children in the street and the common man in the market, and to listen to how they speak.
application: Translation and interface language serve ordinary readers.
limit: One translator’s method; formal-equivalence traditions weigh it differently.

title: Life Together (review)
author: Dietrich Bonhoeffer, 1939 · 9Marks review
takeaway: Written from the Finkenwalde seminary; balances “The Day with Others” (Scripture, song and prayer together) with “The Day Alone” (solitude, silence, meditation), and ends with confession and communion.
application: Holds personal and communal practice together.
limit: Read through a review; quotations are not taken from the text here.

title: The Use of Money (Sermon 50)
author: John Wesley · Wesley Center Online, 1872 edition
takeaway: Three rules: “Gain all you can”, “save all you can”, “give all you can”. Gain is limited by love of neighbour: “This is dear-bought gain. And so is whatever is procured by hurting our neighbour in his soul”.
application: Earning from honest work is not suspect in itself; what matters is whether it harms the person served, and what is done with the gain.
limit: An eighteenth-century sermon on trade and work, not on ministry or apps.

title: The Small Catechism
author: Martin Luther · Book of Concord
takeaway: Each part is headed “As the head of the family should teach them in a simple way to his household”, followed by questions such as “What does this mean?”
application: Teaching the faith to children was given to households first, with short questions and plain answers.
limit: A Lutheran confessional text; other traditions teach children differently.

title: The Life We’re Looking For: Reclaiming Relationship in a Technological World
author: Andy Crouch · Convergent, 2022
takeaway: Argues that persons are made for recognition and love, and that technology’s promise of effortless “superpowers” costs us our humanness.
application: A Christian account of personhood against which to judge companion-like and effortless features.
limit: Read through publisher material and reviews.

title: You Are What You Love: The Spiritual Power of Habit
author: James K. A. Smith · Brazos, 2016
takeaway: Argues that we are formed by what we love, and that habits act as “liturgies”, including “secular liturgies” loaded with a story about who we are.
application: Streaks, badges and feeds are habits that form desire; design them as liturgies.
limit: Read through listings and reviews.

title: Eat This Book: A Conversation in the Art of Spiritual Reading
author: Eugene H. Peterson · Eerdmans, 2006
takeaway: Commends lectio divina and slow, participatory reading of Scripture, and discusses translation from his work on The Message.
application: Supports designs for slow reading and keeping.
limit: Read through the listing.

title: Albert Borgmann (Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy)
author: On Technology and the Character of Contemporary Life · University of Chicago Press, 1984
takeaway: Contrasts the “device paradigm”, which delivers commodities effortlessly, with “focal things and practices” that require attention, engagement and skill; argues technology should support rather than supplant them.
application: A frame for asking whether an app supports the practice of reading and prayer or replaces it.
limit: Philosophy of technology, not theology, though Borgmann wrote as a Catholic.

title: The Way of the Heart: Desert Spirituality and Contemporary Ministry
author: Henri J. M. Nouwen · 1981 · Henri Nouwen Society
takeaway: Draws on the desert fathers and mothers of the fourth and fifth centuries to commend three disciplines, solitude, silence and prayer, as a way out of noise and busyness into a life centred in God.
application: Grounds quiet prayer and silence in a long tradition.
limit: Read through the book page; no quotation used.

title: Parasocial intimacy, change, and nostalgia in podcast listener reviews
author: M. Olguta Vilceanu · Media and Communication 13, 2025
takeaway: A semantic network analysis of over 12,000 podcast reviews found hosts and content central to the trust-based connections listeners form, with nostalgia and attachment showing when hosts or formats change.
application: Hosts become trusted, friend-like voices; name them honestly, and do not let a host’s voice stand in for Scripture or for a pastor.
limit: Reviews of general podcasts, not faith audio.

title: Listening to music for insomnia in adults
author: Jespersen et al. · Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews, 2022
takeaway: 13 trials, 1,007 participants: listening to sedative or relaxing music may improve sleep quality (moderate-certainty evidence); evidence on insomnia severity is very uncertain.
application: Sleep audio can genuinely help; design it to fade into silence rather than to keep someone listening.
limit: Music, not spoken or Scripture content.

title: How the design of YouTube influences user sense of agency
author: Kai Lukoff et al. · CHI 2021
takeaway: In a survey of 120 users, autoplay and recommendations mainly undermined people’s sense of agency, while search and playlists supported it; co-design participants with a specific intention preferred designs that gave them more agency.
application: End sessions and let listeners choose what comes next; do not autoplay.
limit: Video, not devotional audio.

title: Rules of the Band-Societies
author: John Wesley, 25 December 1738 · Holy Joys transcription
takeaway: The design of the meetings is “to obey that command of God, ‘Confess your faults one to another, and pray one for another, that ye may be healed’”; four questions are asked at every meeting, beginning “What known sins have you committed since our last meeting?”
application: Regular self-examination with set questions is an old Christian practice, and it happened among people who knew and prayed for each other, not on a chart.
limit: A small-group discipline for committed members, not a public survey.

title: Natural Church Development Survey
author: Free Methodist Church in Canada · NCD Canada
takeaway: The survey is “completed by 30 people from the congregation chosen according to specific criteria”, measures eight “Quality Characteristics” of church life, and lets leaders “identify the church’s most critical health issues” and track trends over repeated surveys.
application: A church assessment can be anonymous and aggregated, and its result can start a conversation about where to focus.
limit: A denomination’s description of the tool, not an evaluation of it.

title: Book review: Natural Church Development by Christian Schwarz
author: John Ellas and Flavil Yeakley · Journal of the American Society for Church Growth 10(2), 1999
takeaway: Two church-growth researchers welcome the book’s pastoral reach but criticise the research behind its claims, which they call “pseudo-science”.
application: Be modest about what a church score shows; a survey of perceptions is not a measure of health or faithfulness.
limit: A review, from within the church-growth movement.

title: Network: discover your spiritual gifts, personal style and passion
author: Bruce L. Bugbee and Don Cousins · Zondervan, developed with the Willow Creek Association
takeaway: Invites participants to “discover your spiritual gifts, personal style, and God-given passion for serving in the body of Christ”; the course pairs self-assessment with consultants who help people find a place to serve.
application: Gifts assessment has long been tied to serving and to a conversation with another person, not just a result screen.
limit: A publisher’s description.

title: Relationships between personality and spiritual gifts
author: Kenneth J. Stone · Doctor of Psychology dissertation, George Fox University, 1991
takeaway: Compared a spiritual gifts inventory with a five-factor personality measure among church members: personality accounted for about 50% of the shared variance, and Openness and Extraversion correlated with two of three gift factors; the author recommends reconsidering reliance on gift inventories.
application: Present inventory results as what someone enjoys and how they see themselves, and point to serving and to other people for confirmation.
limit: One inventory and one sample.

title: Am I growing yet?
author: Mark Galli · Christianity Today, 25 October 2007
takeaway: Reports on Willow Creek’s Reveal survey, which found that mature believers felt they were “not being fed”, and on the church’s plan to coach “self-feeders” with personal growth plans; Galli asks whether constant self-monitoring of growth serves discipleship.
application: Even careful spiritual measurement raises a theological question: what does tracking one’s own growth do to a person who is meant to look outward?
limit: Commentary on a church’s survey, not a study of apps.

title: Putting feelings into words: affect labeling disrupts amygdala activity in response to affective stimuli
author: Matthew D. Lieberman et al. · Psychological Science 18(5), 2007
takeaway: Labelling the emotion in a picture reduced amygdala response to negative images compared with other ways of processing them, with increased right ventrolateral prefrontal activity.
application: Naming a feeling may help in itself; a check-in can end at the naming, without a score or a chart.
limit: Laboratory study with images, not mood apps.

title: Ecological momentary assessment
author: Saul Shiffman, Arthur A. Stone and Michael R. Hufford · Annual Review of Clinical Psychology 4, 2008
takeaway: Repeatedly sampling people’s current experience in daily life reduces recall bias and reveals patterns, and is used in research and clinical care.
application: Daily check-ins are a recognised method; outside research and care, decide who benefits from the record and how long it should exist.
limit: A method review for researchers and clinicians.

title: The fallacy of personal validation: a classroom demonstration of gullibility
author: Bertram R. Forer · Journal of Abnormal and Social Psychology 44(1), 1949
takeaway: Students rated an identical, generic personality sketch as highly accurate for themselves.
application: Personal-sounding reports feel true whatever their basis; say how a result was produced and what it cannot claim.
limit: A classroom demonstration; later studies refined it.

title: What the Christian app Soultime has discovered with its mood tracker
author: Hope 103.2 · 12 May 2020
takeaway: Soultime described lockdown mood trends across its users and said: “We don’t track people individually, as privacy is very important”.
application: A precedent for using check-ins only in aggregate; say so in the app, and show where individual records are kept.
limit: A news interview; data practices were not independently verified.

title: HelloBible: interactive Bible (App Store listing)
author: HelloBox · Apple App Store
scope: Listing and privacy label reviewed 8 October 2026
takeaway: Describes an experience “tailored to your reality and pace” for students, young adults, parents, people in doubt, Catholics, Protestants, Evangelicals and people without religious affiliation; the privacy label lists contact information and identifiers linked to the user for analytics and personalisation.
application: Personalisation by life situation and church is common; say what each answer changes and what is linked to the person.
limit: A store listing; the onboarding itself was not tested here.

title: Evaluating verifiability in generative search engines
author: Nelson F. Liu, Tianyi Zhang and Percy Liang · Findings of EMNLP 2023
takeaway: Audited answers from four generative search engines: “a mere 51.5% of generated sentences are fully supported by citations and only 74.5% of citations support their associated sentence.”
application: A citation marker is a claim that needs checking, not proof; put the cited words where people can compare them.
limit: General web search engines in 2023, not Bible assistants; systems have changed since.

title: Citations and trust in LLM generated responses
author: Yifan Ding et al. · AAAI 2025
takeaway: Trust rose when answers carried citations, and this “held true even when the citations were random”; trust fell when participants checked the citations.
application: Citations persuade whether or not they support the claim. Make checking easy, and make sure what is cited says what the answer says.
limit: An online experiment with general questions; effects in religious study may differ.

title: Icon usability
author: Aurora Harley · Nielsen Norman Group · 2014
takeaway: Few icons are universally recognised; “Icon labels should be visible at all times”, and hover-only labels fail on touch screens.
application: A row of unlabelled icons under an answer asks people to guess; label them, or keep two or three and put the rest in a labelled menu.
limit: Practitioner guidance from usability testing, not a controlled study.

title: Memory recognition and recall in user interfaces
author: Raluca Budiu · Nielsen Norman Group · 2024
takeaway: “Recognition is easier than recall because it involves more cues”: interfaces that show options ask less of memory than ones that require people to remember and type.
application: Browsing books and chapters asks people to recognise; a reference field asks them to recall. Offer both.
limit: Practitioner guidance drawing on memory research.

title: Understanding SC 3.3.3: Error Suggestion
author: W3C · WCAG 2.2
takeaway: When an input error is detected and suggestions are known, suggest a correction to the user.
application: A reference field should say “Did you mean John 3?” rather than “Not found”, and accept common abbreviations.
limit: A conformance criterion, not a usability study.

title: Understanding SC 2.5.8: Target Size (Minimum)
author: W3C · WCAG 2.2
takeaway: Pointer targets should be at least 24 by 24 CSS pixels, or spaced so that a 24-pixel circle around each does not overlap another.
application: Chapter grids with 150 Psalms and verse grids pack many small targets; size and space them for thumbs.
limit: A minimum, not a recommendation; larger targets help more people.

title: How to pray for intentions on Hallow
author: Hallow help centre
takeaway: Requests are limited to 240 characters, go to friends, a church or groups, can’t be submitted anonymously or edited, and can be kept private, when they are “only saved to your journal and not shared with others”; others respond with a heart.
application: Show the audience, length limit, anonymity and editing rules before someone writes.
limit: The publisher describing its own feature; it does not say whether parish administrators can read requests.

title: Overview of the Church tab
author: Hallow help centre
takeaway: Requests can be posted to friends or a church; “Intentions will remain active for 7 days.”
application: An end date by default keeps old needs from lingering in a feed.
limit: Publisher documentation.

title: Expand your care through confidential member groups
author: Jon Aleixo · Planning Center blog · 28 February 2025
takeaway: Confidential groups hide members from each other, so that “only group leaders will have access to the complete member list”; chat is turned off. The reason given: “Recovery and support groups thrive when participants feel safe enough to attend before eventually opening up.”
application: Support groups can protect members from each other while a named leader stays reachable.
limit: A vendor announcing its own feature; administrators can still see members.

title: YouVersion Prayer
author: YouVersion · bible.com
takeaway: “Keep your prayers private, or invite friends to pray with you.”
application: Private by default, friends by invitation, is the familiar shape for personal requests.
limit: Marketing copy; no help article found on who sees a shared prayer.

title: Clergy juggle prayer requests with privacy rights
author: Amy Green · United Methodist News Service, 2004 · Baltimore-Washington Conference archive
takeaway: After complaints about disclosed information, a church suspended printed prayer requests and then asked for “written approval if the prayer is for someone other than themselves”; a lawyer quoted: “There’s really nothing wrong with getting consent for these kinds of disclosures even when you aren’t legally required to do so.”
application: Ask before naming anyone else, even where the law does not require it.
limit: US practice from 2004, before apps; HIPAA does not bind most congregations.

title: Richtlinie der EKD zum Schutz vor sexualisierter Gewalt (Gewaltschutzrichtlinie)
author: Evangelische Kirche in Deutschland · 18 October 2019, amended 24 June 2022 · as published by the Evangelische Landeskirche in Württemberg
takeaway: Church workers, including volunteers, must report a justified suspicion of sexualised violence without delay to the Melde- und Ansprechstelle (§8), with the confidentiality of their identity protected; pastoral confidentiality and the seal of confession remain untouched. The Melde- und Ansprechstelle is “dem Schutz Betroffener verpflichtet” (§7).
application: A volunteer group leader may not be able to keep a disclosure to themselves; say so before someone shares.
limit: Each Landeskirche implements the guideline in its own law, with different numbering; the EKD planned a revision in 2024. Not a statement of state law.

title: Rahmenordnung Prävention gegen sexualisierte Gewalt
author: Deutsche Bischofskonferenz · in force from 1 January 2020 · as published by the Diocese of Hildesheim
takeaway: Each institution describes how suspicions and complaints are handled, including internal and external advice and reporting routes, which “müssen in geeigneter Weise bekannt gemacht werden”; for every institution “muss eine für Präventionsfragen geschulte Person zur Verfügung stehen”.
application: An app set up for a Catholic parish or institution can show its trained contact and its reporting routes.
limit: A framework; dioceses set the details in their own Präventionsordnungen, and names for the role differ.

title: Parish Safeguarding Officer toolkit
author: Diocese of Durham, Church of England · November 2023
takeaway: With the incumbent, the PCC must appoint at least one Parish Safeguarding Officer, who should be a lay person, and make sure the officer’s contact details are displayed in all church premises.
application: Name the safeguarding officer in an app as a church would on its noticeboard.
limit: One diocese’s toolkit applying national Church of England guidance.

title: Zentrale Anlaufstelle.help
author: Run for the EKD and Diakonie by the independent specialist service of Pfiffigunde Heilbronn e.V.
takeaway: Free advice that is “unabhängig, anonym und unterliegt der Schweigepflicht”; on request it connects people with church and Diakonie contact points, and also informs them about independent alternatives. Phone 0800 5040112.
application: An independent route beside a church’s own contact, for people who will not or cannot go to the church first.
limit: For abuse in Protestant churches and Diakonie in Germany; phone appointments are arranged at set hours.

title: Confidentiality policy
author: thirtyone:eight
takeaway: Personal information “will not be shared outside Thirtyone:eight without explicit and informed consent”, except where someone is at serious and immediate risk, discloses involvement in abuse, or the law requires it.
application: Say what an independent service does with what it hears, including its limits.
limit: A UK charity’s policy; other services set different limits.

title: Study finds agencies can react more supportively than family and friends to victims’ disclosures of sexual assault
author: National Institute of Justice · 30 October 2018 · on research led by Anne P. DePrince
takeaway: Among 228 women, “victims reported receiving more negative reactions from informal supports (e.g., peers, family members) than they experienced when disclosing sexual assault to police or community-based service providers”, and informal supports gave less tangible aid and helpful information.
application: Friends and groups are not automatically the safest listeners for something hard; offer someone trained beside them.
limit: A US study of women disclosing sexual assault; not about churches or apps.

title: Small group participation linked to higher discipleship scores
author: Aaron Earls · Lifeway Research · 4 August 2026
takeaway: US Protestant churchgoers attending a small group five times or more a month scored 74.1 on a discipleship assessment, against 60.4 for those who do not attend one.
application: Groups matter to many people’s faith; design them with care rather than avoid them.
limit: A correlation from self-report; it does not show that groups cause growth. US Protestants only.

title: iOS: Plan with Friends
author: YouVersion Support
takeaway: “When friends join you in a Plan, you see each other’s progress as you finish days. You can talk about each day’s content in a private discussion area.” Up to 300 friends can be invited; “Only the host of the plan can invite others”; the start date can’t be changed once the plan has started; and “if someone leaves a Plan, they cannot rejoin it.”
application: Show participants what the others will see, and give a way back to someone who left or fell behind.
limit: Publisher documentation for iOS; the interface was not tested end to end.

title: iOS: Plan Privacy
author: YouVersion Support
scope: Article reviewed 10 October 2026; the Android article says the same
takeaway: With Friends Only, “your Plan activity (such as completing Plan Days) will be visible to your friends in their Community Feed”; Plan with Friends activity is visible only to participants; “Plan activities on the Community Feed or your timeline cannot be deleted.”
application: Say where each kind of activity appears before it does, and let people delete it.
limit: Publisher documentation; the default setting is not stated.

title: iOS: Plan with Friends – Comments
author: YouVersion Support
takeaway: Each day’s comments sit under “Talk It Over”; others can like a comment with a heart, and a reply to an email notification “becomes part of the day’s comment”. Options on a comment “may include Copy, Edit, and Delete”.
application: A discussion per day gives friends somewhere to talk; say who can step in when a comment hurts someone.
limit: The article does not describe reporting or moderation; it may exist elsewhere in the app.

title: Announcing Plans with Friends
author: YouVersion blog · November 2017
takeaway: “Plans with Friends brings together the best of both”: friends’ perspective “often helps us see things in God’s Word that we might not have noticed on our own”, and “You’ll see one another’s progress as you complete days”.
application: The reason to read together is the conversation; the progress view came with it.
limit: A launch announcement; it gives reasons, not completion figures.

title: A brief history of the Moravian Daily Texts
author: Moravian Church in North America · July 2018
takeaway: “The first printed edition of the Daily Texts (Losungen) was published in Herrnhut, Saxony, in 1731”; since 1788 the watchwords “have been drawn by lot from a collection of around 2,000 suitable Old Testament texts”, while the doctrinal texts are selected.
application: Christians have read the same words on the same day for centuries without anyone counting who read.
limit: A church’s own history of its publication.

title: Anleitung Bibelteilen
author: Erzbistum Köln · 2020
takeaway: The seven steps of Bible sharing (the Lumko method); in step 5, “Jede/r spricht von sich in der ersten Person. Keine Diskussion, kein Vortrag.”
application: Give the conversation a shape: each person says what touched them, and nobody corrects anyone.
limit: One diocese’s leaflet; other versions have six steps or name them differently.

title: Methoden praktischer Bibelarbeit
author: Diözese Linz · Bibelwerk
scope: Section on the Västerås method reviewed 10 October 2026
takeaway: Readers mark verses with a question mark, an exclamation mark (or candle) and an arrow; everyone is invited to bring questions, insights and experiences, and experiences “Ohne Zwang”. Its risks: some verses stay unclear, and “das Problem der ‚Dauerredner‘”.
application: Prompts that invite rather than demand, and a leader who keeps space for quieter voices.
limit: A practical guide, not a study of outcomes.

title: Video calling: safeguarding questions
author: Church of England National Safeguarding Team · April 2020
takeaway: “We strongly recommend reserving video calling for group chats rather than making one-to-one video calls”, applying the guidance Safer Environment and Activities to the online world.
application: With under-18s, keep contact in the group, not one to one.
limit: Written for video calls during the pandemic; the principle comes from wider guidance.

title: Guidance on use of social media and private messaging with young and vulnerable people
author: All Saints Boyne Hill, Church of England parish · 2026
takeaway: “Do not use social visual media for one-to-one conversations with young people - use only within group conversations where a minimum of two DBS checked adults are present.”
application: A group app for under-18s can make two leaders the minimum in any conversation.
limit: One parish’s policy applying diocesan guidance; German churches set their own rules.

title: Social comparison features in physical activity promotion apps: scoping meta-review
author: Danielle Arigo, Megan M. Brown, Kristen Pasko and Jerry Suls · Journal of Medical Internet Research, 2020
takeaway: Improvements from comparison features are “inconsistent”; social comparison “may motivate PA for some people under some circumstances”, and no evidence was found that apps account for people’s “differing preferences for and responses to social comparison information”.
application: Showing everyone’s progress helps some readers and discourages others; let people choose what they see and show.
limit: A review of reviews about physical activity apps, not Bible reading.

title: App Store Review Guidelines
author: Apple
takeaway: “If your app doesn’t include significant account-based features, let people use it without a login. If your app supports account creation, you must also offer account deletion within the app.” Apps “may not require users to enter personal information to function, except when directly relevant to the core functionality of the app or required by law.”
application: Let people read, pray or ask before they sign up, and let them delete the account they make.
limit: Platform rules for the App Store; enforcement varies, and Google Play has its own rules.

title: Human Interface Guidelines: Onboarding
author: Apple
takeaway: Onboarding should be “fast, fun, and optional”; “Postpone nonessential setup flows or customization steps”; “Prefer letting people experience your app or game before prompting them for ratings or purchases.”
application: Open on the content; ask for ratings and payment after people have used the app.
limit: Design guidance, not research.

title: Request runtime permissions
author: Android Developers
takeaway: “Ask for a permission in context, when the user starts to interact with the feature that requires it. Don’t block the user.”
application: Ask for notifications when someone sets a reminder, not at launch.
limit: Platform guidance for Android; Apple’s is similar.

title: Mobile-App Onboarding: An Analysis of Components and Techniques
author: Alita Kendrick · Nielsen Norman Group · 21 June 2020
takeaway: “Skip Onboarding Whenever Possible”; their research on deck-of-cards tutorials “showed that tutorials didn’t improve task performance”; “lengthy promotional onboarding will likely be skipped.”
application: Spend the effort on a clear first screen rather than slides about it.
limit: An expert article drawing on the group’s own studies; details of those studies are in separate reports.

title: Onboarding Tutorials vs. Contextual Help
author: Nielsen Norman Group
takeaway: Tutorials are “dramatically overused”, and “we find that users frequently skip them”; “Users want to start using the product right away.”
application: Teach a feature when someone reaches it, not before the first use.
limit: An expert article; the group notes tutorials can help with genuinely new interactions.

title: Guidelines 03/2022 on deceptive design patterns in social media platform interfaces
author: European Data Protection Board · version 2.0, 14 February 2023
scope: Sections on sign-up and continuous prompting reviewed 11 October 2026
takeaway: “Continuous prompting” occurs “when users are pushed to provide more personal data than necessary for the purposes of processing or to agree with another use of their data, by being repeatedly asked”; at sign-up, users “should understand what exactly they sign up for”.
application: Ask once, for what is needed, and say plainly what someone is signing up for.
limit: Written for social media platforms; it applies the GDPR, which binds other apps too.

title: Cart abandonment rate statistics
author: Baymard Institute
takeaway: Among US online shoppers who abandoned a checkout for reasons other than “just browsing”, 18% gave the reason “The site wanted me to create an account”.
application: A required account turns some people away at the moment they were ready.
limit: Online shopping, not faith apps; a survey of stated reasons.

title: Start with the Bible
author: Diocese of York (Church of England)
takeaway: For someone who has “Picked up a Bible and wondering where to begin”: try Mark; “Start with chapter 1 and read as much as feels manageable. You could also listen to it.” It suggests a short prayer before beginning.
application: A church’s first step asks nothing of the reader: a place to start, and permission to read only a little.
limit: One diocese’s page for newcomers.

title: Help from the Bible
author: The Gideons International in Australia
takeaway: “The front section of all Gideon Bibles and Testaments contains Helps to read the Bible. There are a number of topical indexes to point the reader to what the Bible says about various topics, problems and life situations.”
application: A first page of situations is an old way into Scripture for someone without a reference.
limit: One national association’s description; editions differ.

title: St. Benedict’s Rule for Monasteries
author: Benedict of Nursia, sixth century · Project Gutenberg edition
takeaway: Chapter 53: “Let all guests who arrive be received like Christ.” Chapter 58, on someone asking to join the community: “let him not be granted an easy entrance”.
application: Welcome guests freely; ask for commitment later, from those who want to stay.
limit: A monastic rule; an app is not a monastery, and the analogy is ours.

title: Code of Canon Law, canons 879–958: the Most Holy Eucharist
author: Holy See
takeaway: A priest “is permitted to receive an offering to apply the Mass for a specific intention” (can. 945); those who give it “share its concern to support its ministers and works” (can. 946); and “Any appearance of … trading is to be excluded entirely from the offering for Masses” (can. 947).
application: The church has long let people give for the ministry of the word and sacrament, and drawn a line against trading in it.
limit: Catholic church law; Protestant churches support ministry through offerings, church tax or tithes.

title: The Didache (Teaching of the Twelve Apostles)
author: Early Christian text, late first or early second century · New Advent edition
takeaway: A travelling apostle should “take nothing but bread … but if he ask money, he is a false prophet”; yet “every true prophet that wills to abide among you is worthy of his support. So also a true teacher is himself worthy, as the workman, of his support.”
application: The early church supported its teachers and distrusted those who asked for money: both at once.
limit: An early church manual; its dating and setting are debated.

title: Pricing
author: Anthropic
takeaway: Claude Sonnet 5.5 costs $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens; Claude Haiku 5.5 costs $0.10 and $0.50 for prompts up to 100,000 tokens.
application: Every AI answer has a cost; the choice of model changes it many times over.
limit: One provider’s list prices in US dollars; prices change, and other providers differ.

title: ESV API: introduction
author: Crossway
takeaway: The text is free “for non-commercial use”; a commercial site “is primarily designed to motivate visitors to buy something, to pay for a service, or to give a donation, or it accepts advertising or sponsorships”. Other uses need permission.
application: The translation an app uses can decide whether it may charge or ask for donations at all.
limit: One publisher’s terms; others differ, and the Berean Standard Bible is in the public domain.

title: With 330 million downloads, top Bible app celebrates 10 years
author: Religion News Service · Word&Way, 27 July 2018
takeaway: “An $8.3 million annual budget, funded by Life Church members’ tithes and outside donations, pays for YouVersion”; the app is “free with no commercial advertisements”.
application: A free app is still paid for, here by a church and its donors.
limit: A 2018 report; the current budget is not public in this source.

title: TelefonSeelsorge
author: TelefonSeelsorge Deutschland (Protestant and Catholic churches)
takeaway: “Tag und Nacht erreichbar 0800 1110111 / 0800 1110222 oder 116 123”, by phone, chat or email.
application: A first screen can carry a way to a person, day and night, free of charge.
limit: Germany; other countries have their own services.

title: To grow up healthy, children need to sit less and play more
author: World Health Organization · 24 April 2019
takeaway: For 1-year-olds, sedentary screen time “is not recommended”; for 2-year-olds it “should be no more than 1 hour; less is better”; “When sedentary, engaging in reading and storytelling with a caregiver is encouraged.”
application: For young children, design for a grown-up reading and talking with the child, not for time alone with a screen.
limit: Guidelines for children under 5, about physical activity, sitting and sleep.

title: The New Coviewing: designing for learning through joint media engagement
author: Joan Ganz Cooney Center at Sesame Workshop · 14 February 2012
takeaway: A panel on how young children and “their influencers, from siblings to caregivers to teachers, can view media together”, framed by the report The New Coviewing (Takeuchi and Stevens, 2011). A producer warned that “children may be viewing by themselves” and urged “caution regarding the introduction of material that might be scary or isolating for a child”.
application: Design for watching together, and take care with frightening material a child may meet alone.
limit: A blog report of a panel discussion, not a study.

title: Godly Play
author: Wikipedia, on the method developed by Jerome Berryman
takeaway: Lessons “are taught as stories, illustrated with hands-on materials, which are followed by ‘I wonder’ questions, then by time for students to creatively respond.”
application: Open questions after a story let children make meaning and ask about what troubles them, without a right answer to find.
limit: An encyclopedia summary; Berryman’s own guides are the primary source.

title: App Store Review Guidelines: 1.3 Kids Category
author: Apple
takeaway: Kids Category apps “must not include links out of the app, purchasing opportunities, or other distractions to kids unless reserved for a designated area behind a parental gate”, and “should not include third-party analytics or third-party advertising.”
