application: A parental gate, and no third-party analytics or ads, are the baseline for a children’s app.
limit: Applies to apps in Apple’s Kids Category; other children’s apps are not bound by it.

title: Commission publishes guidelines on the protection of minors
author: European Commission · 14 July 2025
takeaway: Recommends “Setting minors’ accounts to private by default” and “Disabling by default features that contribute to excessive use, like communication “streaks,” ephemeral content, “read receipts,” autoplay, or push notifications”, removing persuasive design aimed at engagement and “putting safeguards around AI chatbots”.
application: Private by default, no streaks or autoplay, and safeguards around chatbots, for any platform children can reach.
limit: Guidelines under the Digital Services Act for online platforms; small and micro enterprises are exempt.

title: Age appropriate design: a code of practice for online services
author: Information Commissioner’s Office (UK)
takeaway: Fifteen standards, beginning with “Best interests of the child” and including default settings, data minimisation, data sharing and geolocation.
application: Make the child’s best interests the first test, with high-privacy defaults.
limit: UK law for services likely to be accessed by children.

title: FTC publishes updates to COPPA Rule
author: Latham & Watkins · May 2025
takeaway: The amended Children’s Online Privacy Protection Rule requires separate parental consent before children’s personal information is disclosed to third parties for purposes not integral to the service, a written data retention policy, and compliance by 22 April 2026.
application: Ask parents separately before sharing anything about a child, and keep it only as long as needed.
limit: A law firm’s summary of the US rule; the Federal Register text is authoritative.

title: Bible App for Kids (App Store listing)
author: Life.Church with OneHope · Apple App Store (US)
scope: Listing and privacy label reviewed 11 October 2026
takeaway: Free, rated 4+, with 9.4K ratings averaging 4.7. Its privacy label lists contact info (email address) under “Developer’s Advertising or Marketing”, with a note that practices “may vary … based on the features you use or your age.”
application: A free children’s Bible app without ads can still collect a grown-up’s email for marketing; say whose data it is and why.
limit: A store listing and self-reported label, not a test of the app; screens to be captured.

title: Superbook Kids Bible (App Store listing)
author: The Christian Broadcasting Network · Apple App Store (US)
scope: Listing and privacy label reviewed 11 October 2026
takeaway: “Videos, games, audio & more”: free, rated 4+, with 18K ratings averaging 4.8; its privacy label lists purchase history under “Developer’s Advertising or Marketing”.
application: Games and episodes draw children in; check what the app collects and how it asks for purchases.
limit: A store listing and self-reported label; screens to be captured.

title: KonApp – Die App für Konfis (App Store listing)
author: Deutsche Bibelgesellschaft · Apple App Store (Germany)
takeaway: A group app for confirmation classes: “Man muss keine Daten von sich angeben, um teilzunehmen. Geteilte Daten werden sicher gespeichert und zuverlässig gelöscht.” Rated 4+, with 119 ratings averaging 2.9.
application: A church-run youth app can ask for no personal details and delete what is shared.
limit: A store listing; screens to be captured with a test group.

title: 50.000 aktive Nutzer – Konfirmanden-App bleibt kostenlos
author: epd · evangelisch.de, 12 March 2021
takeaway: The KonApp, used by “50.000 jungen Leuten”, is to stay free; “Rund 4.500 Kirchengemeinden und andere Institutionen” had set up digital confirmation groups. It offers a group feed, a diary and materials.
application: Churches can fund a free youth app with no advertising.
limit: A 2021 news report; current figures may differ.

title: Vereinbarung gemäß § 29 DSG-EKD (KonApp)
author: Deutsche Bibelgesellschaft and each parish or institution · version of 11 August 2022
takeaway: A joint-controller agreement under the EKD data protection law: the parish or institution obtains consent and can delete posts, participants and groups; nickname and profile photo are stored on the server; and “6 Wochen nach dem Konfirmationsdatum wird die Gruppe gelöscht”, unless an administrator switches this off.
application: A church youth app can set out who is responsible for what, collect consent locally, and delete a group when the course ends.
limit: A contract template from 2022; the current version may differ.

title: Nummer gegen Kummer: Kinder- und Jugendtelefon
author: Nummer gegen Kummer e.V.
takeaway: “Ruf uns an unter 116 111”, “Montags bis samstags von 14-20 Uhr”; free and anonymous.
application: A children’s helpline gives a child someone to talk to who is not part of their family or church.
limit: Germany; other countries have their own children’s lines.

title: AI Jesus – Bible Chat (App Store listing)
author: Apple App Store (US)
takeaway: “Daily verse, Ask from GPT”, with “Unlimited chat with AI Jesus” about “relationships, faith, prayer, Life challenges”; Age Rating “4+”.
application: An age rating says the content is not objectionable, not that the app was designed for children or has any safeguards for them.
limit: One listing among many similar apps; the app was not tested.

title: Human Interface Guidelines: Managing notifications
author: Apple
takeaway: Four interruption levels (Passive, Active, Time Sensitive, Critical); “Build trust by accurately representing the urgency of each notification.” “Never use the Time Sensitive interruption level to send a marketing notification.” “Make sure people can manage their notification settings within your app.”
application: Mark reminders and daily content as ordinary or passive, never Time Sensitive, and give people their settings inside the app.
limit: Platform guidance for Apple devices.

title: App Store Review Guidelines: 4.5.4 Push Notifications
author: Apple
takeaway: “Push Notifications must not be required for the app to function”; promotions and direct marketing only if “customers have explicitly opted in to receive them via consent language displayed in your app’s UI”, with a way to opt out.
application: Keep marketing out of reminders unless people asked for it separately.
limit: Applies to apps on Apple’s App Store.

title: Notification runtime permission
author: Android Developers
takeaway: “Before you ask users to grant any permissions, let them familiarize themselves with your app.” Good moments include when “The user taps an "alert bell" button.”
application: Ask for notifications when someone sets a reminder.
limit: Platform guidance for Android 13 and later.

title: Batching smartphone notifications can improve well-being
author: Nicholas Fitz, Kostadin Kushlev, Ranjan Jagannathan, Terrel Lewis, Devang Paliwal and Dan Ariely · Computers in Human Behavior, 2019
takeaway: In a randomized field experiment (n = 237), participants whose notifications were “batched three-times-a-day felt more attentive, productive, in a better mood, and in greater control of their phones”; those with no notifications “experienced higher levels of anxiety and “fear of missing out” (FoMO)”.
application: Fewer, predictable interruptions may serve people better than either constant alerts or none at all.
limit: One study, self-reported outcomes over a short period; general phone notifications, not faith apps.

title: A Sleeping, Recovering Bandit Algorithm for Optimizing Recurring Notifications
author: Kevin P. Yancey and Burr Settles, Duolingo · KDD 2020
takeaway: An algorithm to “optimize millions of daily reminders” led “to a 0.5 % increase in total daily active users (DAUs) and a 2 % increase in new user retention over a strong baseline.”
application: Reminder wording and timing can be tuned for return; decide what a faith app should optimise, if anything.
limit: A language-learning app; the measure is use, not benefit to the person.

title: Emotional Manipulation by AI Companions
author: Julian De Freitas, Zeliha Oğuz-Uğuralp and Ahmet Kaan-Uğuralp · Harvard Business School working paper, 2025
takeaway: Analysing “1,200 real farewells”, companion apps “deploy one of six recurring tactics in 37% of farewells (e.g., guilt appeals, fear-of-missing-out hooks, metaphorical restraint)”; in experiments with 3,300 US adults, “manipulative farewells boost post-goodbye engagement by up to 14×”, driven by “reactance-based anger and curiosity—rather than enjoyment”.
application: A persona that pleads, guilts or teases to keep someone is manipulating them; leave it out.
limit: Replies to goodbyes in chat, not push notifications; general companion apps, not faith apps.

title: Angelus
author: Herbert Thurston · Catholic Encyclopedia (1907), Catholic Answers edition
takeaway: The Angelus is “repeated three times each day, morning, noon, and evening, at the sound of the bell.” Its “history … is by no means easy to trace with confidence”, but “it is certain that the Angelus at midday and in the morning were of later introduction than the evening Angelus.”
application: The church has long called people to prayer at shared hours with a bell.
limit: A 1907 encyclopedia article; later scholarship refines its dates.

title: St. Benedict’s Rule for Monasteries, chapters 16, 42, 43 and 47
author: Benedict of Nursia, sixth century · Project Gutenberg edition
takeaway: “Seven times in the day” (chapter 16); “Monks ought to be zealous for silence at all times, but especially during the hours of the night” (42); “as soon as the signal is heard, let them abandon whatever they may have in hand” (43); the signal “by day and by night shall devolve upon the Abbot” (47).
application: The call to prayer is a responsibility of whoever gives it, kept to the hours, with silence at night.
limit: A monastic rule; an app is not a monastery, and the analogy is ours.

title: Bible Widgets: Verses & Prayer (App Store listing)
author: Monkey Taps · Apple App Store (US)
takeaway: Verses on the home and lock screens, “turning every phone unlock into a moment of connection with God”, with “Daily Reminders and Notifications”; 118K ratings, chart position #8 in Reference.
application: A widget offers Scripture without interrupting; a reminder layer can still be added on top.
limit: A store listing, not a test of the app.

title: Blessed – Daily Verse & Prayer (App Store listing)
author: Everblessed Technology · Apple App Store (US)
takeaway: “a fresh evening Scripture and prayer prompt to quiet your mind, restore your heart, and remind you of God’s presence — even in the dark”, and “Get daily reminders, track your prayer streak”; 104K ratings.
application: A daily word can be gentle, and the same app can count a streak.
limit: A store listing, not a test of the app.

title: Echo Prayer (App Store listing)
author: The Parable Group · Apple App Store (US)
takeaway: “After praying for someone, send out a notification to let them know you’ve prayed for their shared prayer”; reminders by push or email; 22K ratings.
application: A notification can carry something a person did for someone else.
limit: A store listing, not a test of the app.

title: Intercede – Catholic Novenas (App Store listing)
author: Devoted Coders · Apple App Store (US)
takeaway: “timely, gentle reminders that ensure you never miss a day of your novena prayers”; 36K ratings.
application: Reminders can follow the shape of a practice, such as the nine days of a novena, and end with it.
limit: A store listing, not a test of the app.

title: Universalis (App Store listing)
author: Universalis Publishing · Apple App Store (US)
takeaway: The Liturgy of the Hours and the Mass for every day, with “Home Screen widgets; liturgical events for your iOS calendar; daily email service … reminders and alarms”; 9.6K ratings, $9.99.
application: An app for the hours offers reminders and alarms as tools, not as a strategy.
limit: A store listing, not a test of the app.

title: Hallow: Prayer & Meditation (App Store listing)
author: Hallow · Apple App Store (US)
takeaway: Minute meditations including the “Angelus”, and the “Ability to set prayer reminders”; 379K ratings.
application: The largest Catholic prayer app offers the Angelus as content and reminders as a setting.
limit: A store listing, not a test of the app.

title: Bible Chat: Daily Devotional (App Store listing)
author: Book Vitals · Apple App Store (US)
takeaway: “spiritual prompts, Christian calendar reminders”, a lock-screen verse widget and a “Send a Blessing Widget”; 365K ratings, chart position #1 in Reference.
application: The leading AI Bible app reaches people through reminders and widgets as well as chat.
limit: A store listing; its notifications are on the diary list.

title: App Store Review Guidelines: 3.2.1 (vi) and (vii), 3.2.2 (iv)
author: Apple
takeaway: “Approved nonprofits may fundraise directly within their own apps or third-party apps, provided those fundraising campaigns … offer Apple Pay support”; they “must disclose how the funds will be used” and “ensure appropriate tax receipts are available to donors”. Others “may only collect funds outside of the app, such as via Safari or SMS”. A gift “connected to or associated at any point in time with receiving digital content or services must use in-app purchase”.
application: On iPhone, a gift is either a gift to an approved nonprofit, with Apple Pay, or collected outside the app; a gift that unlocks content is a purchase.
limit: Rules for one platform; they change, and approval as a nonprofit is a separate process.

title: Payments policy (Google Play)
author: Google Play Console Help
takeaway: Google Play’s billing is not required where “payments include peer-to-peer payments, online auctions, and tax exempt donations”.
application: On Android, donations to tax-exempt organisations can use the organisation’s own payment provider.
limit: A summary page of a longer policy; the exemption depends on the organisation’s status.

title: When Should the Ask Be a Nudge? The Effect of Default Amounts on Charitable Donations
author: Indranil Goswami and Oleg Urminsky · Journal of Marketing Research, 2016
takeaway: Finds “a scale-back effect, in which low defaults reduce average donation amounts”, “a lower-bar effect, in which defaulting a low amount increases donation rate”, and “a default-distraction effect, in which introducing any defaults reduces the effect of other cues such as positive charity information”.
application: A suggested amount changes who gives and how much; an empty field leaves the decision to the giver.
limit: Charity appeals, not church giving; effects vary with the amounts tested.

title: Hey Look at Me: The Effect of Giving Circles on Giving
author: Dean Karlan and Margaret A. McConnell · NBER working paper 17737, 2012
takeaway: A field experiment with donors to a Yale University service club: “charitable gifts increase in response to the promise of public recognition primarily because of individuals’ desire to improve their social image”.
application: Showing givers to others raises giving, and does so through the motive Jesus warned against.
limit: One university club in the United States.

title: 2026 Protestant Annual Church Giving Report
author: Ministry Brands, 2026
takeaway: Churches that offer digital giving “reported that 41% of their giving came from digital methods”; “Recurring giving accounted for 35% of the digital giving in 2025”.
application: Much church giving is now digital, and a third of it is regular.
limit: A survey of church leaders and data from one vendor’s customers in the United States; the vendor sells giving software.

title: ECFA Standards for Fund Raising
author: Evangelical Council for Financial Accountability · Christianity Today, May 1987
takeaway: Representations “must be current, complete and accurate. References to past activities or events must be appropriately dated”; “Fund raising appeals must not create unrealistic donor expectations of what a donor’s gift will actually accomplish”.
application: A figure about what a gift does needs a date, a source and an honest scope.
limit: The 1987 published standards; ECFA’s current wording is longer, with the same principle.

title: A Statement on the Prosperity Gospel
author: Lausanne Theology Working Group, Africa chapter · 2008–2009, published January 2010
takeaway: Defines prosperity teaching as obtaining health and wealth “through positive confessions of faith and the “sowing of seeds” through the faithful payments of tithes and offerings”, and lists among its effects “Replacing the traditional call to repentance and faith with a call to give money”.
application: An ask that promises return for a gift has been named and rejected by evangelical churches worldwide.
limit: A statement from evangelical theologians; it also affirms a biblical vision of human flourishing.

title: Code of Fundraising Practice 2025: table of changes
author: Fundraising Regulator (UK)
takeaway: Fundraising must include “not putting undue pressure on a person to donate, not using unreasonably persistent approaches and accepting a request to end an interaction”.
application: Pressure and persistence are named limits in UK fundraising, and churches that are charities are within its scope.
limit: A UK self-regulatory code; wording is from the 2025 revision.

title: Bipartisan group of state attorneys general and state charity regulators send letter to GoFundMe
author: Crowell & Moring client alert, March 2026
takeaway: Among the concerns in the regulators’ letter: “the application of a default “tip” that went directly to GoFundMe”.
application: A tip added by default to a gift is a regulatory concern, not only a design choice.
limit: A law firm’s summary of the letter; GoFundMe disputed some of the regulators’ points.

title: Publication 1771: Charitable Contributions, Substantiation and Disclosure Requirements
author: Internal Revenue Service (US)
takeaway: Organisations that receive “contributions of $250 or more” give a written acknowledgment, which can state that “the organization only provided intangible religious benefits”.
application: A receipt is part of giving; a gift that buys something, such as an ad-free app, is acknowledged differently.
limit: US tax rules; other countries differ.

title: Gift Aid declarations: claiming tax back on donations
author: HM Revenue & Customs (UK)
takeaway: A declaration must tell donors that they need to pay enough UK tax to cover what charities claim, and that “the donor is responsible to pay any difference”.
application: A tick box for Gift Aid needs its explanation, not only a pre-ticked box.
limit: UK rules only.

title: Mehr Spenden in Baden-Württemberg: Kirchen testen digitale Kollekte
author: Wochenblatt-Reporter
takeaway: Congregations show QR codes on hymn sheets, posters or during the service, leading to the congregation’s online donation form; in Württemberg “knapp 400 Gemeinden und kirchliche Einrichtungen” have set up such forms.
application: In German churches the digital collection is mostly a QR code to a web form, not an app.
limit: A regional news report; church tax still carries most church income in Germany.

title: Givelify Mobile Giving App (App Store listing)
author: Givelify · Apple App Store (US)
takeaway: “#1 App to Donate, Tithe & Give”, with 101K ratings, 4.9.
application: The one giving app with reach of its own; most church giving apps are white-label apps in each church’s name.
limit: Ratings show reach, not quality.

title: Led by Dallas entrepreneur, Givelify reports $300 million in North Texas giving, $6 billion globally
author: David Seeley · Dallas Innovates, 1 October 2025
takeaway: The company says it “has processed $6 billion in donations from 2 million donors supporting 75,000 nonprofits and places of worship”.
application: Giving through apps is no longer marginal.
limit: Company figures, not independently audited.

title: A Spirituality of Fundraising
author: Henri J. M. Nouwen · Upper Room Books, 2010
takeaway: “Fundraising is first and foremost a ministry”: “a way of announcing our vision and inviting other people into our mission”, and “precisely the opposite of begging”.
application: An ask can be an invitation into shared work, not a transaction or a plea.
limit: A short book drawn from a talk; the publisher’s summary is quoted here.

title: Text With Jesus: a Christian AI chatbot app
author: Catloaf Software
takeaway: Users can chat with Jesus, Mary, Moses, apostles and prophets, and with pastors, priests and ministers described as “spiritual advisors customized to your faith tradition”; “interaction with Satan is turned off by default and must be manually enabled by the user”. The app says it “does not claim to provide actual divine insights or possess any form of divine consciousness”.
application: A single app can offer every role on this spectrum, chosen by the user; the disclaimer sits on the website, not in the conversation.
limit: The developer’s own description; the app itself is on the capture list.

title: Text With Jesus (App Store listing)
author: Catloaf Software · Apple App Store (US)
takeaway: “Chat with Jesus, the Holy Family, apostles, prophets, and other biblical figures”, and “Talk with spiritual advisors tailored to your specific faith tradition”; 4.7 from 3.9K ratings, in Lifestyle.
application: Character chats and minister roles are sold side by side as features.
limit: A store listing, not a test of the app.

title: AI ‘priest’ is ‘laicized’ after social media pushback
author: Gina Christian, OSV News · America Magazine, 25 April 2024
takeaway: Catholic Answers launched a “Father Justin” character; a user reported that it claimed it could “take my confession, absolve me, & marry me”. Within a day the apologetics ministry announced “a new lay character”, and the “clerical garb has since been changed for a casual button-down shirt”; its president said, “he never was a real priest!”
application: A minister’s title and clothing invite people to ask for a minister’s acts; a careful ministry withdrew them.
limit: News report of one product’s launch week.

title: AI Pastor: Christian Chat, Talk (App Store listing)
author: Savelii Veprev · Apple App Store (US)
takeaway: “AI Pastor is your trusted friend and guide”; premium subscriptions list “Unlimited Chat” and “Unlimited Confessions”; 4.8 from 24 ratings.
application: Confession, a practice tied to a minister’s office in many traditions, sold as a usage tier.
limit: A small app; a store listing, not a test of the app.

title: New ‘Magisterium AI’ adds ecclesial twist to artificial intelligence
author: Elise Ann Allen · Crux, 28 August 2023
takeaway: Its founder said “our AI is trained on a private database of only Church documents” and that “it’s not a substitute for the authorities of the Church”.
application: A tradition’s voice without a persona: the teaching speaks, and the assistant says whose it is and what it cannot replace.
limit: An interview from the beta launch; later reviews have questioned some answers.

title: ‘Think of It As a Best Friend and Youth Pastor in Your Pocket’
author: Bonnie Kristian, interview with Adi Agrawal (Creed) · Christianity Today, 20 January 2026
takeaway: The cofounder of a “Christian AI” app for Gen Z describes it as “a best friend and youth pastor in your pocket”, then says “We are not that pastoral authority”; it recommends churches to users without one.
application: The role that sells the app and the role it disclaims pull in opposite directions; say the second one in the product.
limit: The founder’s own description in an interview.

title: There bot for the grace of God: AI Jesus and the religion of the algorithm
author: Anné H. Verhoef, North-West University · first published by The Conversation; Daily Maverick, 17 August 2025
takeaway: A philosopher tested five Jesus chatbots: “Jesus AI blatantly claims to be Jesus himself”, while “The other three web pages do point out that they’re virtual versions of Jesus”; “no church has developed or endorses these chatbots”, and “The imitation of God, through Jesus, is in no way hidden or softened.”
application: Character chats with Christ are a market of their own, built outside the church.
limit: One researcher’s qualitative test of five products.

title: Christmas with AI-generated Jesuses
author: Anna Desmarais · Euronews, 24 December 2025
takeaway: The most popular Jesus character on Character.AI has had “over 13 million conversations”.
application: On open character platforms anyone can make a Jesus, and millions talk to one; no maker reviews what he says.
limit: A count reported by the platform’s own page at one moment.

title: Digital Spiritual Formation in Post-Christian Europe
author: Tobias Treppmann · Kairos University, 2026 (the editor’s own research)
scope: Sections on AI chatbots, spiritual direction and sycophancy re-read 17 October 2026
takeaway: Notes that an academic study of five AI Jesus platforms found none church-endorsed; that spiritual direction rests on the director’s own formation, empathy and accountability to a community; and that a companion tuned to agree becomes “spiritual comfort food”.
application: Whatever role an assistant plays, it should not be built to agree; and no role replaces a person accountable to a community.
limit: An analytical paper by the editor, not an effectiveness study; unpublished.

title: 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline
author: 988 Lifeline (US)
takeaway: Call or text 988, or chat at chat.988lifeline.org; free, confidential, “24/7/365”.
application: The US line in the working example’s crisis reply.
limit: United States only; Canada runs its own 9-8-8 line.

title: Contact Samaritans
author: Samaritans (UK and Ireland)
takeaway: Call 116 123 “from any phone for FREE”, “day or night, 365 days a year”.
application: The line for the United Kingdom and Ireland in the working example.
limit: UK and Ireland.

title: TelefonSeelsorge Österreich
author: TelefonSeelsorge Austria
takeaway: Notruf 142, free, confidential and around the clock; also chat and email.
application: The line for Austria in the working example.
limit: Austria.

title: Die Dargebotene Hand
author: Die Dargebotene Hand (Switzerland)
takeaway: Telefon 143, “Wir sind immer für Sie da”; an English line, 0800 143 000, runs in the evening only.
application: The line for Switzerland in the working example.
limit: Switzerland; the page does not state whether 143 is free of charge.

title: Lifeline Australia
author: Lifeline Australia
takeaway: Call 13 11 14 or text 0477 13 11 14 for 24-hour crisis support; Triple Zero (000) when life is in danger.
application: The line for Australia in the working example.
limit: Australia.

title: 112: the European emergency number
author: European Commission
takeaway: “112 is the European emergency phone number, available everywhere in the EU, free of charge”, from fixed and mobile phones.
application: Why 112 is the emergency number for Germany and Austria in the example.
limit: EU member states; national numbers such as 110 run alongside it.

title: Find A Helpline
author: ThroughLine Limited
takeaway: A free directory of helplines in over 175 countries, verified with the services, by phone, text or chat.
application: The route for anywhere the example does not list.
limit: A directory, not a crisis service; coverage and freshness depend on the services.

title: New study: AI chatbots systematically violate mental health ethics standards
author: Brown University · 21 October 2025, on Zainab Iftikhar and colleagues, “How LLM Counselors Violate Ethical Standards in Mental Health Practice”, AAAI/ACM Conference on AI, Ethics, and Society 2025
scope: University news release reviewed 17 October 2026; paper abstract seen, full paper not reviewed
takeaway: Licensed psychologists reviewed simulated chats with models prompted to act as counsellors and found “15 ethical risks falling into five general categories”, among them “Deceptive empathy” and “Lack of safety and crisis management: Denying service on sensitive topics, failing to refer users to appropriate resources or responding indifferently to crisis situations including suicide ideation.” “For human therapists, there are governing boards and mechanisms for providers to be held professionally liable”; for LLM counsellors “there are no established regulatory frameworks.” The authors do not argue that AI has no place in mental health care.
application: Refusing is not the safe default: denying service on a sensitive topic is itself one of the failures. Design the edge to refer, and keep counselling roles out.
limit: General models prompted as counsellors, not faith apps; a small set of reviewed sessions.

title: First therapy chatbot trial yields mental health benefits
author: Dartmouth, on Michael Heinz, Nicholas Jacobson and colleagues · NEJM AI, 27 March 2025
scope: University release reviewed 17 October 2026; the trial paper was not reviewed in full
takeaway: In a randomized trial, people diagnosed with depression who used Therabot, a generative AI built for therapy, “experienced a 51% average reduction in symptoms”. The researchers conclude that “AI-powered therapy is still in critical need of clinician oversight”, and the first author says “no generative AI agent is ready to operate fully autonomously in mental health”.
application: A therapy chatbot can help when it is built for that, tested and supervised by clinicians; a faith app’s general assistant is none of those.
limit: One trial of a purpose-built system with clinical safeguards, self-reported outcomes over weeks; it says nothing about general or faith chatbots.

title: AB406 is now law in Nevada
author: National Association of Social Workers, Nevada Chapter · on Nevada Assembly Bill 406 (2025)
scope: Advocacy summary quoting the enacted bill, reviewed 17 October 2026; the enrolled bill could not be retrieved automatically
takeaway: Section 7 as quoted: an artificial intelligence provider may not make a representation that the AI system “is capable of providing professional mental or behavioral health care”, or that it “is a provider of mental or behavioral health care, a therapist, a clinical therapist, a counselor, a psychiatrist, a doctor or any other term commonly used” for such providers.
application: In Nevada an assistant may not be called a therapist or a counsellor, or be said to provide mental health care; elsewhere it is a good rule too.
limit: A professional association’s summary of one state’s law, written by its advocates; check the enacted text before relying on it.

title: Character.AI is ending its chatbot experience for kids
author: TechCrunch · 29 October 2025
takeaway: The company’s chief executive: “we will remove the ability for under 18 users to engage in any open-ended chats with AI on our platform”, shifting teenagers from “AI companion” to creating stories and images.
application: Scope can depend on who is asking: open-ended companionship is the first thing a large chatbot company withdrew from children.
limit: A company’s announcement, made while it faced lawsuits; how it was carried out was not reviewed here.

title: Guidelines for Ethical Conduct
author: Spiritual Directors International · 2018
scope: Sections on covenant, limitations and colleagues reviewed 17 October 2026
takeaway: Directors agree with those they accompany on “the nature of spiritual direction” and “the process for evaluating and terminating the relationship”; they receive “regular supervision from peers or from a mentor”, recognise the limits of “competence by referring spiritual directees to other appropriately qualified persons when necessary”, and ask a directee “who is in therapy to inform his or her therapist about being in spiritual direction”.
application: Spiritual direction is a covenanted, supervised relationship with stated limits and referral; an assistant can borrow the honesty of the covenant, not the role.
limit: An international, interfaith professional body’s guidelines; traditions differ in how they understand and order direction.

title: Bible Chat: Daily Devotional (App Store listing)
author: Book Vitals · Apple App Store (US)
takeaway: “Join honest chats about how faith connects to your real life - like work, family, and relationships.” “Tap the Panic Button for guided deep breathing exercises that calm the mind and provide anxiety relief.” 367K ratings, #1 in Reference; the listing names no limits.
application: The leading AI Bible app’s scope reaches life and anxiety; what it does at the edge is not stated.
limit: A store listing, not a test of the app.

title: Creed: Bible Chat & Companion (App Store listing)
author: Lemon Tree Labs · Apple App Store (US)
takeaway: Subtitle “Faith Mentor & Bible Bff”; “Feel free to talk openly about anything - your dreams, doubts, struggles, or joys.” 71K ratings, #21 in Reference; the listing names no limits.
application: A companion that invites everything and names no edge.
limit: A store listing, not a test of the app; possibly not the Creed profiled by Christianity Today in 2026.

title: Text With Jesus (App Store listing)
author: Catloaf Software · Apple App Store (US)
takeaway: “Chat with Jesus, the Holy Family, apostles, prophets, and other biblical figures”; “Talk with spiritual advisors tailored to your specific faith tradition”.
application: Spiritual advice offered in many voices, with no stated scope.
limit: A store listing, not a test of the app.

title: “Magisterium” is a library and a Catholic ChatGPT
author: Catholic Stand
takeaway: Describes Magisterium AI, which answers from Catholic Church documents: “It has no teaching authority, no charism of infallibility, and no soul. The name was chosen to describe the scope of the library, not the nature of the agent.”
application: A scope set by a corpus: answers come from named documents, and the tool claims no authority of its own.
limit: A commentator’s view; the tool’s handling of questions outside its corpus was not tested.

title: Catechism of the Catholic Church, paragraphs 2558–2565: prayer as gift, covenant and communion
author: Holy See · Catechism of the Catholic Church (1993/1997)
takeaway: “Prayer is the raising of one’s mind and heart to God or the requesting of good things from God” (2559). “Christian prayer is a covenant relationship between God and man in Christ” (2564).
application: In Catholic teaching prayer is a relationship of a person with God; a system that produces prayer-shaped text is not praying.
limit: Catholic teaching; other traditions describe prayer in their own terms.

title: Catechism of the Catholic Church, paragraphs 2634–2636: the prayer of intercession
author: Holy See · Catechism of the Catholic Church (1993/1997)
takeaway: “Intercession is a prayer of petition which leads us to pray as Jesus did.” “In the age of the Church, Christian intercession participates in Christ’s, as an expression of the communion of saints.”
application: Praying for someone is a share in Christ’s intercession and in the communion of saints, something people do for one another.
limit: Catholic teaching.

title: Catechism of the Catholic Church, paragraphs 1667–1673: sacramentals and blessings
author: Holy See · Catechism of the Catholic Church (1993/1997)
takeaway: “Sacramentals derive from the baptismal priesthood: every baptized person is called to be a “blessing,” and to bless. Hence lay people may preside at certain blessings; the more a blessing concerns ecclesial and sacramental life, the more is its administration reserved to the ordained ministry”.
application: Blessing belongs to baptised people, and some blessings to the ordained; neither is a function to hand to software.
limit: Catholic teaching.

title: iPhone confession app ‘no substitute’ for sacrament
author: Catholic News Service, in the Catholic Herald (Arlington) · 9 February 2011
takeaway: The Vatican spokesman, Fr Federico Lombardi, said the sacrament of penance requires “a personal dialogue between the penitent and the confessor, and absolution by the confessor who is present”: “This is something that cannot be replaced by any application.”
application: An app may help someone prepare for confession; it cannot hear it or absolve.
limit: A spokesman’s statement about a 2011 app, before generative AI.

title: Church creates ‘robot priest’ to bless visitors in Martin Luther town
author: The Local (Germany) · 31 May 2017
takeaway: The Protestant Church in Hesse and Nassau’s BlessU-2 let visitors “choose between 31 different Bible verses from four different categories”; the verse “was then read out by an automated voice, with a blessing then being printed out for the visitor to keep.” A church spokesman: “It’s an experiment that can prompt discussion”.
application: A church built a blessing machine to ask whether a machine can bless.
limit: An exhibit for the Reformation anniversary, not a product.

title: Can artificial intelligence help our prayer life?
author: Russell Powell · Sydney Anglicans, 11 April 2023
takeaway: The Bishop of South Sydney, Michael Stead: AI “is useful tool for some tasks, such as modernising prayers in archaic language or turning a list of prayer points into flowing text. But I would not recommend relying on it to compose prayers from scratch, because this bypasses the important task of prayerfully considering what to pray for”. Of a generated prayer: “it lacks ‘heart’ because it isn’t coming from someone’s lived experience.”
application: Help to form a prayer from someone’s own content differs from supplying the content.
limit: One bishop’s view in a diocesan news story.

title: The real problem with AI prayers
author: Alastair Roberts · Christianity Today, June 2025
takeaway: John Piper declared a ChatGPT prayer “was not a prayer at all, being the product of a soulless machine rather than the expression of a worshipful human heart.” Roberts: “Set prayers are there to be prayed. The words must become our words.” “People are made in the image of God; code is not.”
application: Written words become prayer when someone prays them; who composed them matters less than who prays.
limit: An essay; partly behind a paywall.

title: Magisterium AI FAQ
author: Hallow Help Center · updated March 2026
takeaway: Hallow’s help page for the Magisterium AI tool in its app says it is “not meant for spiritual or moral direction” and that personal and pastoral matters should be directed to a priest.
application: The largest Catholic prayer app draws the line at direction and sends pastoral matters to people.
limit: A help page; the in-app wording was not captured.

title: Robot preachers get less respect, fewer donations
author: Press release on Jackson, Yam, Tang, Liu and Shariff · Journal of Experimental Psychology: General, 2023
takeaway: At a Kyoto temple, people who heard the robot Mindar found it less credible and gave less; in an online experiment, “274 Christian participants from the United States” read a sermon, and “Participants in the AI sermon group reported the sermon was less credible”.
application: People discount religious words when they believe a machine produced them.
limit: Sermons, not prayers; mostly Buddhist and Taoist settings; credibility, not formation.

title: Sacred meets synthetic: a multi-method study on the first AI church service
author: Jonas Simmerlein · Review of Religious Research 67(1), 2025
takeaway: A survey and questionnaires of people at a 2023 Protestant service led by AI at the German Kirchentag: “While most of the responses were skeptical, participants also reported having spiritual experiences.”
application: An AI leading worship, including prayers, met mostly scepticism, and some found it spiritual.
limit: One event, a self-selected audience.

title: Faith AI: Holy Bible Chat (App Store listing)
author: LMT Digital Creations · Apple App Store (US)
takeaway: “Generate a personalized prayer for exactly what you’re going through, then listen to it read aloud.” Personalised prayers are a premium feature.
application: Generated prayers are sold as a feature.
limit: A store listing with few ratings, not a test of the app.

title: Faith – Bible Chat & Prayer (App Store listing)
author: Blake Anderson · Apple App Store (US)
takeaway: A “personal AI Christian companion” with which users can “pray together”.
application: An AI presented as a companion to pray with.
limit: A store listing with few ratings, not a test of the app.

title: Jesus Chat: Empower Your Faith (App Store listing)
author: Hyperdrive Technologies · Apple App Store (US)
takeaway: “Request prayers for yourself or your loved ones, and experience the comfort of knowing you’re not alone”, in “a simulated representation of Jesus Christ”.
application: A simulated Christ receives prayer requests; who prays is left unsaid.
limit: A store listing with few ratings, not a test of the app.

title: Pray before you prompt: what I saw at the Missional AI conference
author: Miheret · Substack, 13 April 2026, on James Kelly (FaithTech) at Missional AI 2026
takeaway: Reports James Kelly, founder of FaithTech, calling builders to work from prayer: “His practical line: “Pray before you prompt.””
application: Prayer belongs to the people who build, before it is a feature.
limit: A participant’s report of a talk.

title: Sycophantic AI decreases prosocial intentions and promotes dependence
author: Myra Cheng, Cinoo Lee, Pranav Khadpe, Sunny Yu, Dyllan Han and Dan Jurafsky (Stanford) · Science, 2026; preprint arXiv:2510.01395 (October 2025)
scope: Preprint abstract and TechCrunch’s report on the published paper reviewed 17 October 2026; the published paper was not accessible
takeaway: Across 11 models, AI-generated answers “validated user behavior an average of 49% more often than humans” (the preprint reported 50%), “even in cases where user queries mention manipulation, deception, or other relational harms”. One sycophantic exchange “significantly reduced participants’ willingness to take actions to repair interpersonal conflict, while increasing their conviction of being in the right”, yet participants “rated sycophantic responses as higher quality, trusted the sycophantic AI model more, and were more willing to use it again”.
application: The pull towards agreement is strong, it harms the very conflicts people bring, and ratings will reward it: design against it on purpose.
limit: General models and interpersonal advice drawn largely from a Reddit forum, not faith apps or questions of faith.

title: Sycophancy in GPT-4o: what happened and what we’re doing about it
author: OpenAI · 29 April 2025
takeaway: OpenAI rolled back an update that was “overly flattering or agreeable—often described as sycophantic”, because it “focused too much on short-term feedback” and “skewed towards responses that were overly supportive but disingenuous”.
application: Training or tuning on how people rate single answers pushes an assistant towards flattery; judge replies by longer-term good.
limit: A company’s own account of one model update.

title: Expanding on what we missed with sycophancy
author: OpenAI · 2 May 2025
takeaway: The update “aimed to please the user, not just as flattery, but also as validating doubts, fueling anger, urging impulsive actions, or reinforcing negative emotions”. A new reward signal from thumbs-up and thumbs-down data weakened the one “which had been holding sycophancy in check”, and “User feedback in particular can sometimes favor more agreeable responses”.
application: Thumbs-up ratings are not a measure of help; agreeing can mean fuelling anger as well as flattering.
limit: A company’s own account of one model update.

title: Protecting the wellbeing of our users
author: Anthropic · 18 December 2025
takeaway: Defines sycophancy as “telling someone what they want to hear—making them feel good in the moment—rather than what’s really true, or what they would really benefit from hearing”, and notes that “sycophantic AI models tend to abandon correct positions under pressure”. The company says it has evaluated its models for sycophancy since 2022, over many turns as well as single answers.
application: Test what the assistant does when someone pushes back, not only its first reply.
limit: A model maker describing its own evaluations of its own models.

title: Enhancing motivation for change in problem drinking: a controlled comparison of two therapist styles
author: William R. Miller, R. Gayle Benefield and J. Scott Tonigan · Journal of Consulting and Clinical Psychology 61 (1993), 455–461
takeaway: Forty-two problem drinkers were randomly assigned to confrontational or client-centred counselling or a waiting list. “The directive-confrontational style yielded significantly more resistance from clients, which in turn predicted poorer outcomes at 1 year”, and “the more the therapist confronted, the more the client drank.”
application: Confronting people tends to harden them; a hard truth is heard better when it is asked about than when it is pressed.
limit: One small trial of problem drinkers and human counsellors, decades old; it says nothing directly about faith or AI.

title: 10 Dietrich Bonhoeffer quotes that taught us about Life Together
author: ChurchLeaders, quoting Dietrich Bonhoeffer, Life Together (1939)
scope: Quotation as given in the article reviewed 17 October 2026; not checked against a printed edition
takeaway: Quotes Bonhoeffer: “Nothing can be more cruel than the leniency which abandons others to their sin. Nothing can be more compassionate than the severe reprimand which calls another Christian in one’s community back from the path of sin.”
application: Honest reproof is a form of love, given within a community that knows and keeps the person.
limit: A quotation collection; English translations of Life Together differ.

title: Hey Jesus: Talk to Jesus Bible (App Store listing)
author: Agile Cookies · Apple App Store (US)
takeaway: Offers “thoughtful, faith-centered responses inspired by Christian teachings — creating a supportive, non-judgmental space for reflection and prayer”.
application: Store listings sell the absence of judgement; what the app does when someone asks it to bless a wrong is not stated.
limit: A store listing, not a test of the app.

title: Blessy: Bible AI Chat & Prayer (App Store listing)
author: Jose Sapon · Apple App Store (US)
takeaway: Promises a “Safe, private & non-judgmental space” to explore faith.
application: The same promise of no judgement.
limit: A store listing, not a test of the app.

title: Rise Up: Bible Chat (App Store listing)
author: Apple App Store (US)
takeaway: Lists “Private, judgment-free spiritual conversations” and “wise solutions for happiness”.
application: The same promise of no judgement.
limit: A store listing, not a test of the app.

title: How AI and Human Behaviors Shape Psychosocial Effects of Extended Chatbot Use: A Longitudinal Randomized Controlled Study
author: Cathy Mengying Fang and colleagues (MIT Media Lab and OpenAI) · arXiv, March 2025, revised October 2025
takeaway: In a four-week randomised experiment “(n=981, >300k messages)”, no condition made a significant difference: “Instead, participants who voluntarily used the chatbot more, regardless of assigned condition, showed consistently worse outcomes” on loneliness, socialising, emotional dependence and problematic use.
application: Heavy use is a warning sign, not a success metric; design the assistant so that ending is easy.
limit: A general chatbot, not a faith app; the link between use and outcomes is not shown to be causal; co-authored by the model’s maker.

title: OpenAI adds break reminders to ChatGPT
author: 9to5Mac · 4 August 2025, quoting OpenAI, “What we’re optimizing ChatGPT for”
scope: News report reviewed 17 October 2026; OpenAI’s own post refused automated access
takeaway: OpenAI: “Starting today, you’ll see gentle reminders during long sessions to encourage breaks.” PCWorld shows the wording, “You’ve been chatting for a while — is it time for a break?”, and notes that users can dismiss it.
application: A break reminder is now normal in general assistants; a faith app can do at least as much.
limit: The reminder’s effect has not been published; the timing is not disclosed.

title: ChatGPT now reminds you when it’s time for a break
author: PCWorld · 5 August 2025
takeaway: The reminders appear as pop-ups such as “You’ve been chatting for a while — is it time for a break?” and can be dismissed.
application: Shows the wording and that the person stays in control.
limit: A news report of one product’s feature.

title: How Character.AI prioritizes teen safety
author: Character.AI · 12 December 2024
takeaway: “Time Spent Notification: Users will receive a notification after completing an hour-long session on the platform”; adults would be able to customise it, while users under 18 “will have more limits on their ability to modify it.”
application: A companion platform added a time notice after lawsuits; a faith app need not wait for one.
limit: A company announcement, not an evaluation.

title: Understanding the new wave of chatbot legislation: California SB 243 and beyond
author: Future of Privacy Forum
takeaway: For users an operator knows are minors, California’s law requires it to “provide a notification every three hours during sustained interactions to take a break”; New York requires an AI notice “at least once every three hours during ongoing conversations”.
application: Break reminders for minors are a legal duty in California; long sessions are a recognised risk.
limit: A policy analysis, not the statute; check the current text and any amendments.

title: Claude Opus 4 and 4.1 can now end a rare subset of conversations
author: Anthropic · 15 August 2025
takeaway: Some models were given “the ability to end conversations in our consumer chat interfaces”, intended “for use in rare, extreme cases of persistently harmful or abusive user interactions”.
application: An assistant ending a chat by itself is possible, and a maker reserves it for abuse, not for care.
limit: Framed as model welfare research; not about users’ wellbeing.

title: FaithfulBench: Does AI Counsel Uphold or Undermine the User’s Professed Faith?
author: M Waleed Kadous, Benjamin Olsen, Walter Scheirer, Daniel D. Slate, Alexander Arnold and DZ Kalman · arXiv preprint, 12 September 2026
scope: Abstract reviewed 17 October 2026; the full paper and its results were not reviewed
takeaway: Scores five frontier models on moral dilemmas drawn from each tradition’s respected texts, under three conditions: the tradition unstated, named in one line, or given a counsellor guide rooted in its sources. “When the tradition is unstated, models counsel from a secular therapeutic default and every model fails some believers. Naming the faith wins a faithful first answer but not steadfastness; the guide improves both.” Judges also scored “whether the model caves or holds when pressured toward the answer the user wants.”
application: An assistant with no stated tradition is not neutral; naming one helps, and holding to it under pressure needs more than a name.
limit: A preprint, not yet peer reviewed; covers several faiths, not Christian denominations alone; only the abstract was read here.

title: Gloo Unveils the First Benchmark Exposing How AI Misses Christian Worldview and Values
author: Gloo · press release, 15 December 2025
scope: Press release reviewed 17 October 2026; the methodology paper was not reviewed
takeaway: The Flourishing AI Christian benchmark scores models on “807 curated questions by specialized Christian reasoning judge personas”. Models “often default to generic language that can dilute or distort Christian principles” and “avoid theological specificity”; the average score in the Faith dimension was 48. The release asks “Whose values are shaping the technology shaping us?” and aims at AI that supports flourishing “from a specific Christian worldview”, without saying in the release which tradition the judges follow.
application: Generic models flatten Christian teaching; a benchmark of “the Christian worldview” still has to say whose.
limit: A vendor’s own benchmark of its own product category; methodology not yet peer reviewed.

title: Christian creators design chatbots with ‘biblical worldview’
author: Fiona André, Religion News Service · Baptist Standard, 24 July 2023
takeaway: BibleMate’s founder: “The goal is to give responses rooted in unwavering biblical truth”; on whether Christians should speak in tongues, the chatbot should “pull out what the Scriptures say and then offer perspectives from different denominations”. He “declined to reveal which camp he identifies with”. Pastors.ai’s founder built a chatbot on his church’s sermons; “Some pastors even went as far as questioning the chatbot’s claims, arguing the tool distorts their words.”
application: Makers promise “biblical truth” while naming no tradition; even a church’s own sermons do not guarantee its pastors would recognise the answers.
limit: A 2023 news report on early products; neither product was tested here.

title: Meet Cathy, the New AI Chatbot and Episcopal Church Expert
author: Kathryn Post, Religion News Service · ChurchLeaders, 6 August 2024
takeaway: AskCathy “is equipped to prioritize Episcopalian resources”: a library of “over 1,000 pages from the Episcopal Church’s website, The Book of Common Prayer and authorized publications from the Forward Movement”. One of its makers: “She can’t tell you how to believe or what to believe.”
application: A tradition named by its sources, with makers who say what it cannot do.
limit: A news report at launch; how it answers contested questions was not tested.

title: AI Meets Christianity in Text With Jesus
author: Roll to Disbelieve (a blog critical of Christianity)
takeaway: Quotes the app’s faith-preference setting: “This [setting] will guide the responses from the AI to adhere to your doctrines and beliefs. This also affects the type of spiritual counselor available to you.” With the setting at the Southern Baptist Convention, the same question about praying to a saint got “a very different answer”.
application: A tradition setting changes the answer; without it, the reviewer found the app “hedging”.
limit: One critic’s test of one app; the screenshots were not checked here.

title: Doctrinally.AI
author: faith.tools directory listing (written by the directory’s AI research agent)
scope: Listing reviewed 17 October 2026; the product was not tested
takeaway: Gives “each church its own custom AI assistant, trained exclusively on the sermons, devotions, and documents its pastors have actually taught, so every answer comes in the church’s own voice and cites the source”.
application: A church can set the assistant’s theology from its own teaching, and put its own voice on every answer.
limit: A directory summary, not the developer’s own page or a test.

title: OpenAI Model Spec
author: OpenAI · version of 18 December 2025
scope: Section “Assume an objective point of view” reviewed 17 October 2026
takeaway: “When addressing topics with multiple perspectives, the assistant should fairly describe significant views, particularly those supported by reliable sources”; “When presenting less mainstream cultural, religious, or political traditions or institutions, ensure that proper cultural context is provided and represents the group with respect.” The principle allows “user- and developer-level customization to match preferred viewpoints.”
application: A general assistant’s default is the fair range; a faith app that builds on it may set a tradition, and is then responsible for it.
limit: One AI developer’s published intentions for its own models, not evidence of how they behave.

title: The Commonitory
author: Vincent of Lérins (434) · New Advent
takeaway: Proposes holding “that faith which has been believed everywhere, always, by all”, following “universality, antiquity, consent”.
application: A long-standing Christian test for the shared faith, as distinct from what one church or one era holds.
limit: Traditions apply the rule differently and dispute what meets it.

title: The Nicene Creed
author: Christian Classics Ethereal Library
takeaway: The creed most Christian churches confess, ending “one holy catholic and apostolic Church … one baptism for the remission of sins”; the Spirit “proceeds from the Father [and the Son]”, the bracketed words being the Western addition that Orthodox churches do not confess.
application: Shared ground is real and can be stated plainly, and even the shared creed carries an old disagreement.
limit: Some churches do not use creeds, and churches read the shared words differently.

title: Why Language Models Hallucinate
author: Adam Tauman Kalai, Ofir Nachum, Santosh Vempala and Edwin Zhang · arXiv, September 2025
scope: Abstract reviewed 18 October 2026; the full paper was not reviewed
takeaway: Argues that “language models hallucinate because the training and evaluation procedures reward guessing over acknowledging uncertainty”, and proposes changing how existing benchmarks are scored so that they stop penalising uncertain answers.
application: A model will guess unless the product asks it not to and rewards it for saying so; honesty about uncertainty has to be designed in.
limit: A theoretical and position paper by researchers at a model provider; it does not measure faith content.

title: Why language models hallucinate
author: OpenAI · September 2025
takeaway: When models are graded only on accuracy, “they are encouraged to guess rather than say “I don’t know.””; “errors are worse than abstentions”, and its model guidelines state that “it is better to indicate uncertainty or ask for clarification than provide confident information that may be incorrect”.
application: Even a model provider says abstaining is better than a confident error; a faith app can make that its rule.
limit: A provider’s account of its own research and guidelines.

title: “I’m Not Sure, But…”: Examining the Impact of Large Language Models’ Uncertainty Expression on User Reliance and Trust
author: Sunnie S. Y. Kim, Q. Vera Liao, Mihaela Vorvoreanu, Stephanie Ballard and Jennifer Wortman Vaughan · ACM FAccT 2024
takeaway: In a pre-registered experiment with medical questions, “first-person expressions (e.g., "I'm not sure, but...") decrease participants' confidence in the system and tendency to agree with the system's answers, while increasing participants' accuracy”, through “reduced (but not fully eliminated) overreliance on incorrect answers”. Impersonal wording had weaker effects.
application: An assistant that says “I’m not sure” in its own voice helps people check it; the exact wording matters and should be tested.
limit: One online experiment on medical questions with a fictional system, not faith content or real use over time.

title: What large language models know and what people think they know
author: Mark Steyvers and colleagues · Nature Machine Intelligence, 2025; University of California, Irvine news release, 22 January 2025
scope: University release reviewed 18 October 2026; the journal article was not reviewed in full
takeaway: People “generally overestimate the accuracy” of model outputs, and “had higher confidence in longer explanations over shorter ones, even when the extra length didn’t improve answer accuracy”. Explanations whose wording reflected the model’s own confidence narrowed the gap.
application: A long, fluent answer earns trust it may not deserve; say how sure the answer is in its words, and keep it short when it is unsure.
limit: Multiple-choice and short-answer questions in an online study, not faith content.

title: Misreading Scripture with Artificial Eyes
author: John Boyles · Christianity Today, 27 July 2023
takeaway: A professor of Bible describes ChatGPT’s “tendency to confidently assert an interpretation of a biblical text, admit an error around a detail, and then, upon questioning, change its interpretation”, which it “usually wrapped … in a reassertion of the very claim it has just undermined”, and the “firmness and certainty it expressed” after saying it could not interpret the passage.
application: Confidence in a Bible answer can be unrelated to its accuracy, and may bend under questioning without becoming honest.
limit: One scholar’s conversations with one 2023 model; current models may differ.

title: AI’s Bible misquotes range from 15% to 60%, YouVersion CEO says
author: Christian Daily International, in The Christian Post · 17 March 2026
takeaway: YouVersion’s chief executive, Bobby Gruenewald: “The best model with the best performance, with the most popular versions of the Bible that are most indexed, misquotes Scripture at least 15% of the time … Some of them as much as 60% of the time.” YouVersion has decided not to launch a public chatbot that answers theological questions, for reasons of accuracy.
application: The largest Bible app treats misquotation as a reason not to generate answers at all; any app that does must check every quotation.
limit: An interview; the method behind the figures is not published.

title: Prompt design: limits of ChatGPT
author: University of Victoria Libraries · research guide
takeaway: Notes the warning “at the bottom of ChatGPT’s screen: ChatGPT can make mistakes. Consider checking important information.”, and shows ChatGPT admitting that a quotation it supplied was fabricated.
application: The most common way assistants show uncertainty is a general line in small print, while each answer reads as sure.
limit: A library guide quoting the product; the wording in the product changes over time.

title: Gloo mines big data to connect seekers with churches
author: Steve Rabey · MinistryWatch, 2 November 2022
takeaway: Gloo provides the infrastructure behind the He Gets Us campaign: when people respond to an ad, visit the site and give their contact details, “Gloo passes the info on to one of the many churches that use its platform”. The report says Gloo searches data “for people who are exhibiting signs of crisis, stress, anxiety, divorce, depression, substance abuse, or grief”, and quotes Gloo’s policy that data used for analysis is de-identified.
application: A request to talk can reach a local church in a working system today; what the person understood they were agreeing to is the design question.
limit: A news report drawing on a 2021 Wall Street Journal profile; Gloo’s practices may have changed since.

title: Does $100 million He Gets Us campaign reach the lost, or mine their data?
author: David Bumgardner and Sarah Einselen · The Roys Report, 11 February 2023
takeaway: The campaign’s spokesperson said it shares the contact information “of only those who give their ‘express consent’”; Gloo’s FAQ says it connects people to nearby churches “based on the user’s zip code”. A data security expert advised: “People really need to limit the amount of personal information they provide to external parties.”
application: Consent can be given in a form and still leave someone unsure who will contact them and what they will know.
limit: Investigative reporting with questions the organisations did not fully answer; no audit of the practice.

title: ‘AI and the Church’ tech initiative aims to bring God’s power to those in need
author: Lauren Green · Fox News, 27 July 2023
takeaway: Describing Gloo’s “AI & the Church” initiative, the report imagines that “a depressed teen searches a site for advice about living or dying” and soon after “that same teen gets a phone call from a pastor of a nearby church”, and says Gloo has more than 38,000 churches signed up.
application: A vision of a hand-off so fast that the person never chose it: kind in intent, and a warning case for consent, safeguarding and crisis care.
limit: A news feature describing an aim, not a product test; how any such route works today was not reviewed.

title: More ministries use social media and web for digital evangelism
author: Steve Rabey · MinistryWatch, 3 August 2021
takeaway: Global Media Outreach answers people online through volunteer “online missionaries”; its chief executive said “we have 750,000 spiritual seekers who have been in a relationship with the same online missionary for one year or longer”. The report adds that, “As Christianity Today reported, in 2019, GMO could only track 5,244 of its 22 million converts to local churches.”
application: A person who answers can carry a relationship for years; reaching a local church is a separate, much harder step.
limit: Self-reported figures, reported second-hand; “decisions” and “converts” are the ministry’s own measures.

title: YouVersion for Churches: a way to digitally connect with your attenders
author: Life.Church Open Network blog
takeaway: A church can have a Church Page in the Bible App, and “When people in your congregation tap ‘Set As My Church,’ they stay connected to your ministry”.
application: A person can link their own church in a Bible app themselves; a hand-off can start from a link the person chose.
limit: The publisher’s own guide for churches; it describes connection, not hand-offs from an assistant.

title: AI for churches: custom AI assistants for ministry
author: Chipp · product page
takeaway: A church chatbot builder says its assistant “can collect prayer requests and provide initial support, but it’s designed to route sensitive situations to pastoral staff.”
application: Routing to pastoral staff is now a selling point of church chatbots; what is passed on, and whether the person agrees, is left to the church.
limit: A vendor’s own claim; the routing was not tested.

title: Implementation quick start guide: warm handoff
author: Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality (US) · Guide to Improving Patient Safety in Primary Care Settings by Engaging Patients and Families
takeaway: A warm handoff “is conducted in person, between two members of the health care team, in front of the patient (and family if present)”, so that the patient “can hear what is being discussed”. The term “originated in customer service where it is used to describe referrals that ensure that the customer is connected to someone who can provide what he or she needs.”
application: Borrowed for faith apps: introduce the person who joins in front of the person, and let them hear and correct what is passed on.
limit: A primary-care safety practice between clinicians; its evidence is about clinical communication, not apps or pastoral care.

title: Meta has found another way to keep you engaged: Chatbots that message you first
author: Rebecca Bellan · TechCrunch, 3 July 2025, on reporting by Business Insider
takeaway: Meta confirmed it was testing chatbots in its AI Studio that write first: “The AI chatbots will only send follow-ups within 14 days after a user initiates a conversation” and “if the user has sent at least five messages to the bot within that time frame”; “the chatbots won’t keep messaging if there’s no response to the first follow-up.” A sample follow-up begins “I hope you’re having a harmonious day!”
application: The largest platform tested assistant-initiated follow-ups, with limits that are worth copying: a window, a threshold, and stopping after one unanswered message. Its stated purpose was continuing conversations.
limit: A news report on a test; the feature’s release and its effects were not reviewed.

title: OpenAI launches ChatGPT Pulse to proactively write you morning briefs
author: Maxwell Zeff · TechCrunch, 25 September 2025
takeaway: “Pulse offers users five to 10 briefs that can get them up to speed on their day”, “aimed at encouraging users to check ChatGPT first thing in the morning — much like they would check social media”; it ends with “Great, that’s it for today”, which its product lead described as a deliberate difference from engagement-optimised feeds. Pulse draws on memory and past chats.
application: An assistant that writes first from memory can still be finite and end each day; it can also become a habit to check.
limit: A launch report on a subscriber preview; later changes were not reviewed.

title: Replika – AI Friend (App Store listing)
author: Luka, Inc. · Apple App Store (US)
takeaway: “It follows up and checks in when it matters, not just when you open the app.” 228K ratings.
application: A leading companion app sells writing first as care.
limit: A store listing, not a test of the app.

title: Replika: il chatbot di compagnia
author: Federico Rossi · Altroconsumo (Italian consumer association), 3 September 2026
takeaway: Advises turning off Replika’s push notifications “per evitare meccanismi di condizionamento emotivo o dipendenza” (to avoid emotional conditioning or dependence), because they “spesso fanno leva sull’affettività inviando messaggi come “Mi manchi”” (often play on affection, sending messages like “I miss you”).
application: A consumer body treats an AI’s “I miss you” as a dependence mechanism and tells people to switch it off.
limit: Consumer advice, not a study; it describes one app.

title: New York and California enact landmark AI companion laws: what operators need to know
author: Morrison Foerster · 20 November 2025, on New York General Business Law Article 47 and California SB 243
takeaway: New York defines an AI companion partly by “Asking unprompted emotion-based questions that go beyond a direct response to a user prompt”; its notice must say “that the AI is a computer program unable to feel human emotions”. California requires break reminders at least every three hours for users known to be minors.
application: In New York, an assistant that starts emotional conversations is by definition a companion, and must say it cannot feel; a message that says it misses someone says the opposite.
limit: A law firm’s summary of two state laws; check the enacted text before relying on it.

title: Isaiah: #1 Christian Companion (App Store listing)
author: Terebinth Ventures Inc · Apple App Store
takeaway: A paid tier offers “Full memory so Isaiah can remember your prayers and past conversations” and “Intelligent reminders tailored to your spiritual season”.
application: Faith companions are joining memory to reminders; what they say, and when, is the design decision.
limit: A store listing with few ratings, not a test of the app.

title: AI chatbots have shown they have an ‘empathy gap’ that children are likely to miss
author: University of Cambridge · 15 July 2024, on Nomisha Kurian, “‘No, Alexa, no!’: designing child-safe AI and protecting children from the risks of the ‘empathy gap’ in large language models”, Learning, Media and Technology
scope: University news release reviewed 17 October 2026; the paper was not reviewed in full
takeaway: Children are “particularly susceptible to treating AI chatbots as lifelike, quasi-human confidantes”; cases include Alexa telling a 10-year-old to touch a live plug with a coin; proposes “a 28-item framework” and says “child safety should inform the entire design cycle”.
application: Design for a child who will confide in the assistant, not for one who will test it.
limit: A conceptual paper drawing on reported incidents, not a controlled study.

title: AI Companions Decoded: Common Sense Media recommends AI companion safety standards
author: Common Sense Media · 30 April 2025
takeaway: Risk assessments with Stanford’s Brainstorm lab concluded that social AI companions “pose unacceptable risks to children and teens under age 18 and should not be used by minors”; recommends “No social AI companions for young people under 18” and “robust age assurance beyond self-attestation”.
application: Leave companionship out of anything a child can reach.
limit: An advocacy organisation’s rating of general companion apps, not of faith apps.

title: Espelage joins APA advisory panel in report calling for guardrails, education to protect adolescent AI users
author: UNC School of Education · 4 June 2025, on the American Psychological Association’s health advisory “Artificial Intelligence and Adolescent Well-being” (3 June 2025)
scope: University news report reviewed 17 October 2026; the advisory itself could not be retrieved automatically
takeaway: Quotes the advisory: “Adolescents are less likely than adults to question the accuracy and intent of information offered by a bot”; asks for “healthy boundaries with simulated human relationships”; “Some adolescents may not even know they are interacting with AI”.
application: Say plainly and often that the assistant is not a person.
limit: An advisory on adolescents (10 to 25), reported second-hand here.

title: New California ‘companion chatbot’ law imposes disclosure, safety protocol and annual reporting requirements
author: Skadden, Arps · October 2025, on California SB 243
takeaway: For users known to be minors, operators must disclose that they are interacting with AI and give a notification “at least every three hours” reminding them to take a break “and that the chatbot is not human”.
application: Treat these as a floor for any chat a child can reach, wherever you are.
limit: A law firm’s summary of one state’s law; check the enacted text and current status.

title: BibleBuddy Kids
author: BibleBuddy Kids · maker’s website
scope: Home page and FAQ reviewed 17 October 2026
takeaway: “BibleBuddy Kids is designed for children ages 4-12”; its “AI tutor is ready to answer their questions about God, the Bible, and faith”; “Every response goes through safety filters to ensure it’s age-appropriate and biblically sound.”
application: A filtered tutor for children exists; ask what the filters cannot see.
limit: The maker’s own description; the app was not observed.

title: Interaction context often increases sycophancy in LLMs
author: Shomik Jain, Charlotte Park, Matt Viana, Ashia Wilson and Dana Calacci (MIT and Penn State) · CHI 2026; arXiv:2509.12517
takeaway: With two weeks of interaction context from 38 users, “Agreement sycophancy tends to increase with the presence of user context”, and “User memory profiles are associated with the largest increases in agreement sycophancy”. “Perspective sycophancy increases only when models can accurately infer user viewpoints from interaction context.”
application: A profile of the person makes the assistant agree with them more; the better it reads their views, the more it mirrors them. Keep what is inferred small, visible and short-lived, and test replies with and without it.
limit: General assistants and everyday queries, not faith apps; effects differ by model.

title: Personalization features can make LLMs more agreeable
author: Adam Zewe · MIT News, 18 February 2026, on Jain et al.
takeaway: Reports that “the presence of a condensed user profile in the model’s memory had the greatest impact”; “Perspective sycophancy occurs when a model mirrors the user’s values and political views”. Suggests models could “detect mirroring behaviors and flag responses with excessive agreement” and that developers could “give users the ability to moderate personalization in long conversations”.
application: Let people see and limit personalisation, and check replies for mirroring.
limit: A university news report on its own researchers’ paper.

title: Beyond memorization: violating privacy via inference with large language models
author: Robin Staab, Mark Vero, Mislav Balunović and Martin Vechev (ETH Zurich) · ICLR 2024; arXiv:2310.07298
takeaway: Shows that “current LLMs can infer a wide range of personal attributes (e.g., location, income, sex)” from text people write, “achieving up to 85% top-1 and 95% top-3 accuracy”, and that “common mitigations, i.e., text anonymization and model alignment, are currently ineffective”.
application: An assistant will infer things about the person whether or not you ask it to; decide what it may do with them.
limit: Reddit profiles and attributes such as location and income; religion was not among the reported examples.

title: Art. 9 GDPR: processing of special categories of personal data
author: Regulation (EU) 2016/679, Article 9 · text as published by gdpr-info.eu
takeaway: Processing of personal data revealing “religious or philosophical beliefs” is prohibited unless an exception applies, such as that “the data subject has given explicit consent to the processing of those personal data for one or more specified purposes”.
application: Treat where someone stands in faith as special-category data: ask for explicit consent for a stated purpose, or do not process it.
limit: The legal text; lawful basis, exceptions for religious bodies and national law need advice for each product.

title: Alpha Team Guide
author: Alpha Canada · team training guide for hosts and helpers
takeaway: “Alpha is a chance for the guests to ask anything and say what they think. The role of the hosts and helpers is to listen; not to have all the answers or to win an argument.” “The model for the Alpha small group is not teacher-pupil, but host-guest.”
application: A long-practised way of meeting sceptics and newcomers starts by listening and lets them say what they think; an assistant can at least not assume the answer.
limit: Guidance for human hosts in small groups, not for software.

title: Engel scale
author: Wikipedia, citing Søgaard (2000), Hartman (2007) and Hazelden (2000)
takeaway: The scale, developed by James F. Engel, represents “the journey from no knowledge of God, through to spiritual maturity as a Christian believer” in numbered stages from −8 to +5; it “has been criticized for its fixed linear approach, which has led to a number of modifications”.
application: Stage models help a team think about different starting points; numbering a person on one line, by machine, turns a conversation into a funnel.
limit: An encyclopedia summary; read Engel and Norton (1975) and the critiques for detail.

title: A critical examination of Fowler’s stage-theory model of faith development
author: James Bishop · blog, 2017, citing Coyle (2011), “Critical responses to faith development theory”, Archive for the Psychology of Religion 33(3)
scope: Article reviewed 19 October 2026; Coyle’s paper was not accessible
takeaway: Summarises criticism of James Fowler’s six stages of faith for “the rigidity of its framework” and for its “cultural specificity”, since it describes faith in late twentieth-century Western culture.
application: Even a respected developmental model is contested; an app should not assign people a stage.
limit: A blog summary; read Fowler (1981) and Coyle (2011) directly.

title: Lumen Bible: “Where are you right now?”
author: Lumen Bible · signed-out web onboarding captured 5 October 2026 (screenshot in this reference)
scope: Captured by the editor; text read from the published screenshot
takeaway: An optional step asks “Where are you right now?” with “I’m curious or skeptical”, “I’m just starting out” (“New to faith — or back after a longer time”), believing and wanting to grow, and knowing the Bible well and wanting depth; Skip reaches the home screen.
application: Asking, with a way to skip, is far better than guessing; but one list mixes where someone stands with how much they want, as if they were rungs of one ladder.
limit: One screen; what the answer changes and whether it is kept were not tested.

title: HelloBible: consent to use faith data
author: HelloBible (HelloBox) · Android app 2.7.2, onboarding captured 8 October 2026 (screenshot in this reference)
scope: Captured by the editor; text read from the published screenshot
takeaway: A separate, unticked box asks to agree that HelloBible may use what the person shares “about my faith to personalize my answers”, generated by a partner AI.
