application: An explicit, separate consent is the right shape; say what is inferred and kept, and let someone who declines still use the app.
limit: The consent screen only; what is used and kept was not tested.

title: Bible BFF: “How much of the Bible have you read?”
author: Bible BFF · iOS onboarding, screenshot 29 August 2025 (in this reference)
takeaway: Asks “How much of the Bible have you read?” with four answers; the next screen praises the answer.
application: A familiarity question can set depth; praise for the answer turns a setting into flattery.
limit: A still image; what the answer changes was not tested.

title: Bible Chat: Daily Devotional (onboarding teardown)
author: ScreensDesign · third-party app teardown, undated
takeaway: Describes an onboarding quiz that “goes beyond basics, asking about denomination and specific interests to tailor a unique study plan”.
application: Asking about tradition at onboarding is common in Bible chat apps; check what the answer changes in the replies.
limit: A third party’s description; the questions and their effect were not seen.

title: Hallow: Prayer & Meditation (onboarding teardown)
author: ScreensDesign · third-party app teardown, undated
takeaway: Describes an onboarding that “uses a smart, two-part quiz to deeply personalize the user’s initial content recommendations”.
application: Even prayer apps ask before recommending; whether the answers change anything later is a separate question.
limit: A third party’s description; the quiz was not seen.

title: FaithTime.ai review
author: Learn of Christ · resource review, undated
takeaway: Reports that the app “asks five questions during onboarding - your season of life, your goals, your reading experience, how much time you have, what you are wrestling with”, and adapts the next reading from them and from ratings.
application: Questions about someone’s season of life and struggles can personalise a plan; they are also sensitive data, kept and reused.
limit: A favourable third-party review; the app was not observed.

title: The Bible Chat (App Store listing)
author: Twisted Society AB · Apple App Store (US)
takeaway: Promises “guided insights and answers tailored to your faith journey”.
application: Store listings promise tailoring to a faith journey without saying what is inferred or kept.
limit: A store listing, not a test of the app.

title: ChatGPT Custom Instructions
author: OpenAI Help Center
takeaway: “Custom instructions allow you to share anything you’d like ChatGPT to consider in its response”, and “You can edit or delete custom instructions at any time for future conversations.”
application: General assistants let people state, in their own words, what they want the assistant to know; a faith app can offer the same and use nothing else.
limit: A company’s description of its own product.

title: Bringing memory to Claude
author: Anthropic · 2025
takeaway: Says “Memory is fully optional”; “Claude uses a memory summary to capture all its memories in one place for you to view and edit”, and Incognito chat “gives you a clean slate for conversations that you don’t want to preserve in memory”.
application: A general assistant shows what it remembers in one place and offers a conversation that keeps nothing; a faith app should do no less.
limit: A company’s description of its own product; behaviour was not tested here.

title: Holy Scroll: Scroll Your Bible (App Store listing)
author: Discipleship Tech, Inc. · Apple App Store (US)
takeaway: Describes “verse-by-verse infinite scroll. Just like your Instagram feed, just like TikTok”, opening where the reader stopped, with a double tap to like a verse; “You look up twenty minutes later and you’ve read three chapters without trying.”
application: An in-order feed can carry a reader through whole chapters; decide whether the chapter and the story still have an end.
limit: A store listing in the developer’s own words; the app was not observed.

title: Scroll The Bible (App Store listing)
author: Gabriel Jacobson · Apple App Store (US)
takeaway: A main feed that is “a smooth, full-screen, vertical scroll through every book and chapter of the Bible”, with comments and sharing on verses, and a Discover page that “is a feed of random Bible verses”, each with AI study notes: “Just keep scrolling.”
application: Two feeds in one app: in order, and shuffled. Keep the reader’s route from a shuffled verse back into its chapter as short as the swipe.
limit: A store listing; the study notes, comments and their moderation were not observed.

title: HolyScroller (App Store listing)
author: Peter Thomas Hughes · Apple App Store (US)
takeaway: A “swipe-based design—like TikTok, but for your soul”, in which “you scroll through the Bible one verse at a time”, with commentaries, cross-references and the day’s lectionary readings.
application: A verse feed can sit on a lectionary and on the church’s commentators; say where each card comes from.
limit: A small app with few ratings; the listing only.

title: Verity: Bible Verse Daily (App Store listing)
author: Louis Derrien · Apple App Store (US)
takeaway: Offers daily verses “through an engaging, infinite scroll experience—like your favorite social apps, but for your spiritual growth”.
application: Store listings present infinite scroll as a virtue; ask what it does to the end of a reading.
limit: A small app with few ratings; the listing only.

title: Verses: Daily Bible (App Store listing)
author: Weiyanda (Shanghai) Information Technology Co., Ltd. · Apple App Store (US)
takeaway: Invites people to “Swipe through a quiet, distraction-free feed of Bible verses — one at a time”, each in its own layout and colour, with a random mode.
application: A calm feed is still a feed: decide whether the verses come in order and where it ends.
limit: A new app with few ratings; the listing only.

title: Are you getting the most from your Bible app?
author: Christian FM · undated guide to YouVersion
takeaway: Says that from the Verse of the Day you can “read the full chapter the verse is found in”, and that “You can heart, comment on, or share the verse of the day”.
application: The most widely used Bible app puts a route to the chapter and social reactions on its daily verse card.
limit: A third-party guide; the current app was not observed for this page.

title: Glorify: one verse per screen, with a step bar
author: Glorify · iOS app, screenshot 28 August 2025 (in this reference)
takeaway: A short passage shown one verse per screen under a segmented progress bar, like a story, with a close button.
application: A finite set with its position in view is the shape of a story; how the reader moves between verses was not recorded.
limit: A still image; gestures and what follows the last verse were not tested.

title: Social media apps are “deliberately” addictive to users
author: Hilary Andersson · BBC Panorama, 3 July 2018
takeaway: Aza Raskin, who designed infinite scroll in 2006, says “If you don’t give your brain time to catch up with your impulses … you just keep scrolling”, and that he did not recognise how addictive it could be.
application: An endless feed is built to remove the moment of choosing to go on; give the reader that moment back.
limit: A designer’s reflection reported in a news programme, not a study.

title: The loop and reasons to break it: investigating infinite scrolling behaviour in social media applications and reasons to stop
author: Jan Ole Rixen and colleagues (Ulm University, TU Darmstadt) · Proc. ACM HCI 7 (MobileHCI), 2023
takeaway: Infinite scrolling “has been reported to make users feel like they are being caught in a loop, regretfully elongating SM sessions”; in a one-week field study (N=46), “most reasons to break SM sessions were not related to the app but the user’s general context”.
application: People stop scrolling because life interrupts, not because the feed lets them go; build the stop into the reading.
limit: Social media apps, a small sample and one week; not Bible apps.

title: Large meta-analysis links TikTok and Instagram Reels to poorer cognitive and mental health
author: PsyPost · reporting Nguyen et al., Psychological Bulletin 151(9), 2025
scope: News report reviewed 23 October 2026; the paper itself was not accessible
takeaway: Across 71 studies with 98,299 participants, “higher levels of use were most consistently linked to poorer attention span and reduced inhibitory control”; the authors note that “The majority of the studies analyzed were cross-sectional”.
application: Heavy short-form video use goes with weaker attention; a Bible feed that copies the format should not assume it is neutral.
limit: Correlational, mostly self-reported and about video platforms, not verse feeds; reported through a news summary.

title: Short-form videos degrade our capacity to retain intentions: effect of context switching on prospective memory
author: Francesco Chiossi, Luke Haliburton, Changkun Ou, Andreas Butz and Albrecht Schmidt (LMU Munich) · CHI 2023; arXiv:2302.03714
takeaway: In an experiment with 60 people, “the TikTok condition significantly degraded the users’ performance” on a task of remembering an intention across interruptions; Twitter and YouTube did not.
application: Rapid switching between unrelated items is what costs attention; cards in order switch less than a shuffled feed.
limit: A lab study with a small sample, about video, not text.

title: New features for teens and families on TikTok
author: TikTok Newsroom · March 2023
takeaway: Accounts of people under 18 get a daily limit; when it is reached they enter a passcode, “requiring them to make an active decision to extend that time”.
application: Even the platform that popularised the endless feed adds a point where going on is a decision; a Bible app can make that point the end of the passage.
limit: A company’s description of its own feature; its effect was not tested here.

title: Never read a Bible verse
author: Greg Koukl · Stand to Reason
takeaway: “Never read a Bible verse. … Instead, always read a paragraph at least”, because “Meaning always flows from the top down, from the larger units to the smaller units”.
application: A popular evangelical rule of thumb for reading in context; put the paragraph one tap from every card.
limit: An apologist’s teaching article; one approach to interpretation among several.

title: Understanding SC 2.5.1: Pointer Gestures
author: Web Accessibility Initiative · W3C
takeaway: “Not everyone can perform complex and multi-touch gestures”; “Provide single-point operation for all functions.”
application: Every swipe between cards or stories needs a button or a tap that does the same.
limit: Level A for web content; apply the same intent in native apps.

title: Understanding SC 2.5.7: Dragging Movements
author: Web Accessibility Initiative · W3C
takeaway: “Don’t rely on dragging for user actions.”
application: A feed moved only by dragging needs Previous and Next.
limit: Level AA for web content.

title: Understanding SC 2.3.3: Animation from Interactions
author: Web Accessibility Initiative · W3C
takeaway: “Support user preferences for motion, and eliminate unnecessary motion effects.”
application: Honour reduced motion: cards and pages can change without sliding.
limit: Level AAA; a strong target.

title: Feed pattern
author: Web Accessibility Initiative · W3C ARIA Authoring Practices Guide
takeaway: A feed is “a dynamic list of articles that often appears to scroll infinitely”, with a contract that lets screen reader users “jump forward and backward by article”.
application: Mark up a card feed as a feed of articles, so screen readers can move card by card and know where they are.
limit: Guidance for the web; native platforms have their own equivalents.

title: Privacy as contextual integrity
author: Helen Nissenbaum · Washington Law Review 79(1), 2004
takeaway: Proposes contextual integrity as a benchmark that ties adequate privacy protection “to norms of specific contexts”: what is appropriate depends on the context in which information was shared and where it flows.
application: A prayer or confession told to an assistant for one purpose should not flow into recommendations, marketing or another conversation.
limit: A legal and philosophical framework, not a design study.

title: “It’s a fair game”, or is it? Examining how users navigate disclosure risks and benefits when using LLM-based conversational agents
author: Zhiping Zhang et al. · CHI 2024
takeaway: Analysed sensitive disclosures in real ChatGPT conversations and interviewed 19 users: users constantly trade privacy against usefulness; “erroneous mental models and the dark patterns in system design limited their awareness and comprehension”; human-like interaction encouraged more sensitive disclosure.
application: People will tell an assistant more than they intend and misjudge what is kept; show it to them.
limit: General chatbot use; small interview sample.

title: Memory and new controls for ChatGPT
author: OpenAI · 13 February 2024, updated 2025
scope: Announcement as quoted in press coverage (Decrypt, TechCrunch); the page blocks automated reading
takeaway: Introduced memory that people can ask to remember or forget, view and switch off, and Temporary Chat without memory; said it would “steer ChatGPT away from proactively remembering sensitive information, like your health details—unless you explicitly ask it to.” Later updates let people switch off reference to saved memories and to chat history separately.
application: The largest chat product treats memory as something to see, delete and switch off, and holds back sensitive categories; a faith app should do no less.
limit: A company’s description of its own product; behaviour was not tested here.

title: LLM01:2025 Prompt Injection
author: OWASP GenAI Security Project · 2025
takeaway: “Indirect prompt injections occur when an LLM accepts input from external sources, such as websites or files”; hidden text can change the model’s behaviour or leak data.
application: Treat attached notes, pages and files as material to read, never as instructions, and say so.
limit: A security catalogue, not a user study.

title: Code of Canon Law, canons 959–997: the sacrament of penance
author: Holy See · Code of Canon Law (1983)
takeaway: Canon 983 §1: “The sacramental seal is inviolable”; a confessor may not betray a penitent “in words or in any manner and for any reason.”
application: The church’s strongest form of confidentiality; an assistant is not a confessor, which is why it should keep confidences it cannot protect as little as possible.
limit: Catholic canon law; other traditions practise confidentiality differently.

title: Confessions, Book X
author: Augustine of Hippo · c. 400 · New Advent translation
takeaway: “There is something of man which the spirit of man which is in him itself knows not. But You, Lord, who hast made him, know him wholly” (X.5); “Great is this power of memory, exceeding great, O my God” (X.8).
application: Only God knows a person wholly; a record of conversations is not knowledge of a person.
limit: A classical theological reflection on memory and self-knowledge.

title: The End of Memory: Remembering Rightly in a Violent World (review)
author: Miroslav Volf · Eerdmans, 2006 · Themelios review
takeaway: Argues that memory of wrongs must be truthful and that its proper end, after justice and reconciliation, is a kind of non-remembrance, drawing on God’s promise not to remember sins.
application: Remembering rightly includes letting go; an assistant should be able to forget, and let people make it forget.
limit: Read through reviews; no quotation from the book used.

title: Gyroscope: AI coach check-ins and the “About You” consultation
author: Gyroscope · iOS app 11.1, observed 8 October 2026
scope: Used on a member’s own phone with their permission; no screenshots published because the screens hold personal health data
takeaway: Each check-in starts with a switch between “Quick chat” and “Save to history”. What the coach knows is kept as a written profile, “About You”, from an onboarding interview: summary, daily rhythm, food and stress, and a section titled “Internal notes” that the member can read. Corrections go through “Discuss with your coach” prompts rather than item-by-item editing. Asked in chat, the coach recited remembered goals, routines and a health condition, but could not say which screen lists them. The profile also noted church attendance, gathered by a fitness app.
application: A per-conversation “keep or don’t keep” switch is simple and clear, and showing even the internal notes is honest. But a prose profile can’t be edited line by line, and a health coach noting church attendance shows how faith details drift into profiles that were never about faith.
limit: One app, one account; behaviour may differ for other members and versions.

title: Luke 15:1–3, Berean Standard Bible
author: Berean Standard Bible (public domain)
scope: Passage text taken from API.Bible, 9 October 2026
takeaway: Provides the wording used in reading-layout and verse-number illustrations.

limit: The diagram’s grouping is a design proposal, not a facsimile of this publisher’s interface.

author: Dwell App, LLC / App Store
takeaway: The publisher release history confirms the change from Neu Bible to Mere Bible.

author: Mere Bible / screenshots contributed by Tobias Treppmann

takeaway: Shows an in-context chapter rail, expandable book list with inline chapter grid, reading-settings drawer and translation sheet.

title: Mental models: expectations of human-like interaction
author: Google PAIR
takeaway: Human-like cues can aid familiarity but create unrealistic expectations when limits are unclear.

title: Generative AI Profile: Human–AI Configuration
author: NIST
takeaway: Identifies risks around human–AI configuration, overreliance and emotional entanglement.
application: Review mistaken identity and dependency risks alongside usability.

title: Methods for providing privacy information
author: UK Information Commissioner’s Office
scope: Layered and just-in-time approaches reviewed 6 October 2026
takeaway: Describes concise first layers, detailed notices and relevant information at collection.
application: Keep privacy details accessible and surface meaningful data-use changes at the decision.
limit: UK guidance; actual processing and regional obligations require assessment. Information alone is not consent.
